orig_integration_power_integrals.description: Reverse power and chain rules, keep the original real domain, and use definite bounds or endpoint limits only when they are valid.

sections.title: How do I reverse differentiation?
sections.label: The reverse power rule
sections.intro: An antiderivative \(F\) of \(f\) satisfies \(F^{\prime}(x)=f(x)\). An indefinite integral describes the family of these functions. The expression inside the integral is the integrand, and \(\mathrm{d}x\) names the variable of integration.

blocks.html:
\[\int kx^n\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{kx^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\qquad n\ne-1.\]

Increase the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent. Integrate sums term by term. A constant integrates as \(\int k\,\mathrm{d}x=kx+C\).

blocks.title: Reverse each power and keep the constant
blocks.prompt: Write \(\int(8x^3-6x+7)\,\mathrm{d}x\) as \(Ax^4+Bx^2+Dx+C\). Find \(A,B,D\), where \(C\) is an arbitrary constant.
blocks.hint: Increase each power by one, divide its coefficient by the new power and integrate the constant term as a multiple of \(x\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\int(8x^3-6x+7)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{8x^4}{4}-\frac{6x^2}{2}+7x+C.\]
  2. \[=2x^4-3x^2+7x+C.\]

  3. Differentiating gives \(8x^3-6x+7\), so the coefficients are \(2,-3,7\).

blocks.html: Keep \(+C\) in an indefinite integral. The rule excludes \(n=-1\), since it would divide by zero. The integral of \(x^{-1}\) requires a different rule; do not write \(\frac{x^0}{0}\).
Differentiate your antiderivative to check it. You should recover the complete original integrand, including every coefficient and sign.

sections.title: How do I rewrite roots and fractions without losing the domain?
sections.label: Rewrite and retain restrictions
sections.intro: Expand finite polynomial products when needed, or divide every numerator term by the denominator. Convert roots and reciprocals into rational powers, then use the same power rule. Do not integrate the numerator and denominator separately.

blocks.title: Divide every numerator term by the denominator
blocks.prompt: Write an antiderivative of \(\frac{2x^2+3}{\sqrt{x}}\) as \(Ax^{\frac{5}{2}}+Bx^{\frac{1}{2}}+C\). Find \(A,B\) and choose the original real domain.
blocks.hint: Rewrite the integrand as \(2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+3x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\). The square-root denominator must be real and nonzero.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\int\left(2x^{\frac{3}{2}}+3x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{4}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}}+6x^{\frac{1}{2}}+C.\]

  2. The original domain is \(x>0\). Although the antiderivative formula has a finite value at zero, the original integrand is not defined there.

blocks.html: Use the original real domain. An even root requires a nonnegative input; a denominator must also be nonzero. Odd roots can have negative inputs. For rational powers with odd denominator, use the real odd root, as in \(x^{\frac{4}{3}}=(\sqrt[3]{x})^4\).

Algebraic cancellation does not restore a missing input. For example, \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\) only when \(x\ne1\). Its antiderivative is \(\frac{x^2}{2}+x+C\) on each interval separated by \(1\); the constants on those intervals may differ.
A simpler antiderivative may be defined at more inputs than the original integrand. Keep the original exclusions, and inspect any excluded point before using definite bounds that reach or cross it.

sections.title: How do I integrate a power of a linear expression?
sections.label: Reverse the inner factor
sections.intro: Differentiating a power of \(ax+b\) multiplies by \(a\). Reversing that process requires division by \(a\), as well as division by the new outer exponent.

blocks.html:
\[\int k(ax+b)^n\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{k(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C,\qquad a\ne0,\ n\ne-1.\]

Use this on intervals where the original integrand is real and defined. A negative \(a\) keeps its sign in the denominator.

1. For the integral of \((2x+3)^3\), try \(F(x)=K(2x+3)^4+C\).
  2. \[F'(x)=K\cdot4(2x+3)^3\cdot2=8K(2x+3)^3.\]The outer derivative contributes \(4\) and the inner derivative contributes \(2\).
  3. Matching the integrand gives \(8K=1\implies K=\frac18\).\[\int(2x+3)^3\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{(2x+3)^4}{8}+C.\]

Differentiating \(\frac{(2x+3)^4}{8}+C\) recovers \((2x+3)^3\): the outer factor \(4\) and inner factor \(2\) cancel the denominator.

blocks.title: Divide by the negative inner gradient
blocks.prompt: For \(x\ne5\), write \(\int(5-x)^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x=A(5-x)^p+C\). Find \(A,p\).
blocks.hint: The new exponent is \(-1\), and the inner derivative is also \(-1\). Divide by both.

blocks.html: If \(a=0\), first treat the integrand as the constant \(kb^n\). When that is a finite real number, its integral is \(kb^n x+C\). The nonconstant linear-power formula is unnecessary and would divide by zero.
The formula does not apply unchanged to a nonlinear inner expression. For example, expand \((x^2+1)^2=x^4+2x^2+1\), then integrate to get \(\frac{x^5}{5}+\frac{2x^3}{3}+x+C\).

sections.title: How do I evaluate a definite integral?
sections.label: Bounds and signed values
sections.intro: For a continuous integrand on a finite closed interval, find an antiderivative first and then subtract its lower-bound value from its upper-bound value. This gives a number, not an arbitrary family.

blocks.html:
\[\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[F(x)\right]_a^b=F(b)-F(a),\qquad F^{\prime}=f.\]

The constants cancel, so no \(+C\) remains in the definite value. Put brackets around the whole lower-bound substitution before subtracting.

blocks.title: Substitute upper minus lower and reverse the sign when needed
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(I=\int_0^2(3x^2-4x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x\), then the same integral with its bounds reversed.

fields.label: Integral from the upper bound back to the lower bound

blocks.hint: An antiderivative is \(x^3-2x^2+x\). Substitute into this whole expression before subtracting.

blocks.html:
When all relevant integrals exist, the following rules hold:

\[\int_b^a f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=-\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad\int_a^a f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=0.\]\[\int_a^c f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_b^c f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

You can also take constant factors outside an integral and add or subtract integrals term by term.
Keep exact fractions and radicals until the final answer. A definite integral represents signed accumulation. Geometric area requires attention to where the graph lies above or below the axis.

sections.title: What if a bound is infinite or the integrand is undefined?
sections.label: Improper integrals
sections.intro: An infinite interval or an unbounded integrand requires an improper integral. An excluded endpoint must also be checked by a limit. Replace the problematic endpoint by a valid finite value, evaluate there, and then approach the endpoint. A finite limit means the integral converges; otherwise it diverges.

blocks.html:
\[\int_0^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\int_{\varepsilon}^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad b>0.\]\[\int_a^{\infty}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_a^R f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

For an improper upper finite endpoint, approach it from the left. For a lower endpoint of negative infinity, send a finite lower bound toward negative infinity. Each required limit must be finite.

Both curves rise without bound near zero. For \(\varepsilon>0\), evaluate the two areas before letting \(\varepsilon\to0^+\). The plots use different vertical scales.

\[\int_\varepsilon^1 x^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}x=2(1-\sqrt\varepsilon)\longrightarrow2.\]\[\int_\varepsilon^1 x^{-3/2}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}-1\right)\longrightarrow+\infty.\]

Both curves become unbounded near zero. Yet \(\int_0^1x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\), while \(\int_0^1x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) diverges. The limit of the accumulated integral decides.

blocks.title: An undefined endpoint can converge or diverge
blocks.prompt: Find the improper integral \(\int_0^9x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). Then decide whether \(\int_0^1x^{-\frac{4}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) converges or diverges.
blocks.hint: Replace zero by \(\varepsilon>0\), integrate, then take the limit as \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\int_{\varepsilon}^9x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=6-2\sqrt{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow6.\]
  2. \[\int_{\varepsilon}^1x^{-\frac{4}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-3x^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right]_{\varepsilon}^1=-3+3\varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{3}}\longrightarrow+\infty.\]

  3. The first integral converges to \(6\); the second has no finite value and diverges.

blocks.html: At an interior excluded point \(c\), split into a left and a right integral. Take the one-sided limits separately. Add the results only if both are finite. Do the same at every singularity; endpoint subtraction across the whole interval is not enough.

blocks.title: An interior singularity needs two separate finite limits
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{8}\frac{1}{(\sqrt[3]{x})^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) as an improper integral. The cube root is the real cube root. Give the left contribution up to zero, the right contribution from zero and their sum.
blocks.hint: The integrand is undefined at zero. On each side an antiderivative is \(3\sqrt[3]{x}\); evaluate the two one-sided limits independently.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\lim_{u\to0^-}\int_{-1}^{u}x^{-\frac{2}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{u\to0^-}\left(3\sqrt[3]{u}+3\right)=3.\]
  2. \[\lim_{v\to0^+}\int_v^8x^{-\frac{2}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{v\to0^+}\left(6-3\sqrt[3]{v}\right)=6.\]

  3. Both contributions have finite limits, so the improper integral exists and equals \(3+6=9\).

blocks.html: Do not cancel positive and negative divergences or treat infinity as an ordinary endpoint value. A finite-looking answer from \(F(b)-F(a)\) does not establish convergence across an excluded input.

glossary.definition: The function or expression inside the integration symbol.
A function \(F\) whose derivative is the given function \(f\).
The arbitrary constant \(C\) in a family of antiderivatives.
A signed accumulation over stated bounds, with a numerical value when it exists.
An integral requiring a limit because the interval is infinite or the original integrand has a problematic point.
Having a finite limit for every required improper contribution.
Failing to have the required finite improper-integral value.
The remaining contribution beyond a finite upper cutoff.

examples.title: Check an indefinite integral by differentiating
examples.question: Find \(\int(6x^2-4x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
solution:
Integrate the three terms separately:

\[\int(6x^2-4x+3)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{6x^3}{3}-\frac{4x^2}{2}+3x+C.\]

Differentiate the result:

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(2x^3-2x^2+3x+C\right)=6x^2-4x+3.\]
Every constant \(C\) disappears on differentiation, so the indefinite integral is a family of functions.

examples.title: Rewrite a quotient as separate powers
examples.question: For \(x>0\), find \(\int\frac{5x^2+6}{\sqrt{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
solution:
Divide each numerator term by \(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\):

\[\frac{5x^2+6}{\sqrt{x}}=5x^{\frac{3}{2}}+6x^{-\frac{1}{2}}.\]
The constant of integration does not change the original restriction from the denominator.

examples.title: Use real cube roots for negative inputs
examples.question: Find an antiderivative of \(4\sqrt[3]{x}\) valid for real inputs. Check its derivative at \(x=-8\).
solution: Here \(x^{\frac{4}{3}}\) means \((\sqrt[3]{x})^4\), using the real cube root. It is defined for negative as well as positive inputs.
At zero, \(F(x)=3|x|^{\frac{4}{3}}+C\) also has derivative zero, matching the continuous integrand. The formula therefore works across the whole real line.

examples.title: Reverse both parts of the chain rule
examples.question: Find \(\int(2x+3)^3\,\mathrm{d}x\) without expanding.
solution:
Increase the outer exponent to \(4\), divide by \(4\), then divide by the inner derivative \(2\):

\[\int(2x+3)^3\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{(2x+3)^4}{8}+C.\]

Check by differentiating the proposed antiderivative:

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{(2x+3)^4}{8}\right)=\frac{1}{8}\cdot4(2x+3)^3\cdot2=(2x+3)^3.\]
Without the extra division by \(2\), the derivative would be twice the required integrand.

examples.title: A definite integral can be negative
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_{-1}^{2}(2x-3)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
solution: The integrand is continuous over the whole interval. An antiderivative is \(F(x)=x^2-3x\).
This is signed accumulation, so a negative answer is possible. The constant cancels in \((F(2)+C)-(F(-1)+C)\).

examples.title: Compare two powers at an improper lower endpoint
examples.question: Determine whether \(\int_0^1x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\int_0^1x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) converge. Find any finite value.
solution: Neither integrand is defined at zero. Replace that endpoint by \(\varepsilon>0\) before evaluating.
\[\int_{\varepsilon}^1x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_{\varepsilon}^1=2-2\sqrt{\varepsilon}\longrightarrow2.\]
The first improper integral converges to \(2\), even though the curve becomes unbounded near zero.
\[\int_{\varepsilon}^1x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{\varepsilon}^1=2\varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}}-2\longrightarrow+\infty.\]
The second integral diverges: the limit is not finite. Infinity is not a number to substitute into an antiderivative.

examples.title: Replace an infinite endpoint by a finite bound first
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_2^{\infty}3x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x\). If it is approximated by integrating only up to \(R\ge2\), find the smallest integer \(R\) that leaves a tail less than \(0.1\).
solution: \[\int_2^R3x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-\frac{3}{x}\right]_2^R=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3}{R}.\]
\[\lim_{R\to\infty}\left(\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3}{R}\right)=\frac{3}{2}.\]

The remaining tail is the difference from this finite total:

\[\int_R^{\infty}3x^{-2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{3}{R}.\]

\[\frac{3}{R}<0.1\Longrightarrow R>30.\]

The smallest integer is \(31\); \(R=30\) gives equality and fails the strict inequality.
A different power need not converge at infinity. For example, \(\int_1^R x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=2\sqrt{R}-2\) grows without bound.

examples.title: Never cancel two divergent contributions across a singularity
examples.question: Does \(\int_{-1}^{1}x^{-3}\,\mathrm{d}x\) exist as an improper integral?
solution: Zero is inside the interval and is excluded from the integrand. Split there and take the limits independently.
\[\lim_{u\to0^-}\int_{-1}^{u}x^{-3}\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{u\to0^-}\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2u^2}\right)=-\infty.\]
\[\lim_{v\to0^+}\int_v^1x^{-3}\,\mathrm{d}x=\lim_{v\to0^+}\left(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2v^2}\right)=+\infty.\]
Both one-sided integrals must have finite values for their sum to define the ordinary improper integral. They do not, so the integral diverges.
Formal endpoint subtraction using \(-\frac{1}{2x^2}\) would give zero. That calculation crosses an interior singularity and is invalid; opposite divergences cannot be cancelled.

extraPractice.title: Reverse each derivative and keep the constant
extraPractice.prompt: Write the general antiderivative of \(12x^2-6x+5\) as \(Ax^3+Bx^2+Dx+C\). Find \(A,B,D\). Explain on paper why the arbitrary constant is needed.
extraPractice.hint: Increase each power by one and divide by its new value. A constant integrand is a multiple of \(x^0\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\int(12x^2-6x+5)\,\mathrm{d}x=4x^3-3x^2+5x+C.\]

  2. Differentiation returns \(12x^2-6x+5\). Every constant has derivative zero, so the derivative does not determine \(C\).

extraPractice.title: Rewrite a quotient before integrating
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), express \(\displaystyle\int\frac{6x^3+3\sqrt{x}}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) in the form \(Ax^2+Bx^{-\frac{1}{2}}+C\). Find \(A,B\).
extraPractice.hint: Divide each numerator term by \(x^2\); the second power becomes \(-\frac{3}{2}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{6x^3+3\sqrt{x}}{x^2}=6x+3x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\qquad(x>0).\]
  2. \[\int\left(6x+3x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x=3x^2-6x^{-\frac{1}{2}}+C.\]

  3. Differentiate to check: the second coefficient becomes \((-6)\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=3\), with power \(-\frac{3}{2}\). The original domain stays \(x>0\).

extraPractice.title: Undo a negative inner multiplier
extraPractice.prompt: Find \(K,m\) such that \(\displaystyle\int5(3-2x)^4\,\mathrm{d}x=K(3-2x)^m+C\).

retry.feedback: You divided by the new power. Also divide by the inner derivative \(-2\).
The inner derivative is negative; keep that sign in the divisor.

extraPractice.hint: The new power is \(5\). The derivative of the inside is \(-2\), so the divisor includes both factors.

extraPractice.title: Use brackets, reverse limits and join intervals
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=3x^2-4x\). Find \(I=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(J=\displaystyle\int_{1}^{-2}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\). You are also given \(\displaystyle\int_1^3f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=10\). Use this to find \(K=\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{3}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
extraPractice.hint: An antiderivative is \(x^3-2x^2\). Put brackets around the whole lower-endpoint value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[I=\left[x^3-2x^2\right]_{-2}^{1}=(-1)-(-16)=15.\]
  2. \[J=-I=-15.\]
  3. \[K=\int_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_1^3f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=15+10=25.\]

  4. These are signed integrals. No change of sign is made merely because part of the curve is below the axis.

extraPractice.title: Use the real cube root on negative inputs
extraPractice.prompt: Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{-8}^{-1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\mathrm{d}x\) exactly. Interpret fractional powers through the real cube root.
extraPractice.hint: An antiderivative is \(\frac{3}{4}(\sqrt[3]{x})^4\). The integrand is negative throughout this interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[F(x)=\frac{3}{4}\left(\sqrt[3]{x}\right)^4=\frac{3}{4}x^{\frac{4}{3}}.\]
  2. \[F(-1)=\frac{3}{4},\qquad F(-8)=\frac{3}{4}(-2)^4=12.\]
  3. \[\int_{-8}^{-1}\sqrt[3]{x}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{3}{4}-12=-\frac{45}{4}.\]

  4. The sign agrees with the graph lying below the horizontal axis. A calculator that rejects a negative base raised to a fractional power should be used with the real cube-root expression instead.

extraPractice.title: Check the assumptions before applying a formula
extraPractice.prompt:
Answer each separate question.

(a) Find the coefficient of \(x\) in \(\displaystyle\int(0x+4)^3\,\mathrm{d}x\).

(b) Does the power rule \(\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\) apply when \(n=-1\)?

(c) After simplifying \(\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\), is the original excluded input restored?

options.no: No: its divisor would be zero.
options.yes: Yes: the answer is a constant.

extraPractice.hint: Treat a constant inside expression directly. A simplified formula has to keep restrictions from its original expression.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(0x+4)^3=64\Longrightarrow\int64\,\mathrm{d}x=64x+C.\]

  2. The linear-inner formula assumes a nonzero coefficient of \(x\). It is unnecessary here. The ordinary power formula also requires \(n\ne-1\), since otherwise its denominator is zero.

  3. \[\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}=x+1\qquad(x\ne1).\]

  4. An antiderivative on either side of the missing input is \(\frac{x^2}{2}+x+C\). The constants on the two separate intervals need not be the same; algebraic cancellation does not restore the original domain.

starters.title: Two unbounded integrands can behave differently
starters.question:
Decide whether each improper integral has a finite value. For the first, give the exact value if it converges. Justify both conclusions using a lower endpoint \(\varepsilon>0\) before taking a one-sided limit.

\[I=\int_0^4x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad J=\int_0^4x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
starters.hint: Integrate on \([\varepsilon,4]\), where both functions are defined. Examine the lower-endpoint term as \(\varepsilon\) approaches zero from above.
starters.solution:
1. \[I=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_{\varepsilon}^{4}=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}(4-2\sqrt{\varepsilon})=4.\]

  2. The first integral converges even though the integrand becomes unbounded near zero.

  3. \[\int_{\varepsilon}^{4}x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{\varepsilon}^{4}=-1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}.\]

  4. As \(\varepsilon\to0^+\), the last expression grows without bound. Thus \(J\) diverges to positive infinity; infinity is not a finite integral value.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: replace the first zero endpoint by a positive lower bound and state the limit.
  • 1 mark: obtain the first antiderivative \(2\sqrt{x}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the finite value and conclusion.
  • 1 mark: obtain the second antiderivative \(-2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\).
  • 1 mark: evaluate the second truncated integral with the correct sign.
  • 1 mark: justify positive divergence from its lower-endpoint term.

starters.title: An infinite interval can have a finite integral
starters.question: Evaluate \(\displaystyle I=\int_1^{\infty}\frac{6}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\). For \(R\ge1\), write the remaining tail \(\displaystyle T(R)=\int_R^{\infty}\frac{6}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x\) as \(\frac{k}{R}\). Find \(k\), then find the least integer \(R\) for which \(T(R)<0.05\).
starters.hint: Use a finite upper bound \(M\), then take \(M\to\infty\). The final inequality is strict.
starters.solution:
1. \[I=\lim_{M\to\infty}\left[-\frac{6}{x}\right]_1^M=\lim_{M\to\infty}\left(6-\frac{6}{M}\right)=6.\]
  2. \[T(R)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\left(-\frac{6}{M}+\frac{6}{R}\right)=\frac{6}{R}.\]
  3. \[\frac{6}{R}<0.05\Longleftrightarrow R>120\qquad(R>0).\]

  4. The least integer is \(121\). At \(R=120\), the tail equals \(0.05\) and does not satisfy the strict inequality.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: replace infinity by a finite upper bound and state a limit.
  • 1 mark: obtain the antiderivative \(-\frac{6}{x}\).
  • 1 mark: obtain the convergent total.
  • 1 mark: derive the tail \(\frac{6}{R}\).
  • 1 mark: solve the strict inequality correctly.
  • 1 mark: select the least allowed integer and exclude equality.

starters.title: Do not cross a singularity using endpoint subtraction
starters.question:
A student writes

\[\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1}=-2.\]

Identify the singular input. For \(\varepsilon>0\), express the left and right truncated integrals in the form \(\frac{A}{\varepsilon}+B\) and \(\frac{D}{\varepsilon}+E\). Decide whether the original improper integral converges.
starters.hint: Split at zero. Use intervals \([-1,-\varepsilon]\) and \([\varepsilon,1]\), and evaluate each separately.
starters.solution:
1. The integrand is undefined at \(x=0\), inside the interval. The ordinary endpoint-subtraction argument does not apply across this singularity.

  2. \[\int_{-1}^{-\varepsilon}\frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{-\varepsilon}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}-1.\]
  3. \[\int_{\varepsilon}^{1}\frac{1}{x^2}\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{\varepsilon}^{1}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}-1.\]

  4. Each expression tends to positive infinity as its endpoint approaches zero from the relevant side. An improper integral across an interior singularity converges only if both one-sided integrals converge separately. Here they do not, so there is no finite integral value.

  5. The integrand is positive wherever defined. That also flags the student’s negative result as impossible, but the split limit calculation supplies the proof of divergence.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: identify the internal singularity and explain why ordinary endpoint subtraction is invalid.
  • 1 mark: split into two appropriate one-sided integrals.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the left truncated integral.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the right truncated integral.
  • 1 mark: justify divergence of each one-sided limit.
  • 1 mark: state the resulting divergence of the full improper integral.

revision.body:
Integrate first, check the domain, then evaluate valid bounds or take the necessary limits.

Reverse the power rule

\[\int kx^n\,\mathrm{d}x= rac{kx^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\qquad n e-1.\]

Integrate sums term by term; \(\int k\,\mathrm{d}x=kx+C\). Rewrite roots and quotients as powers. Keep the original domain and use real odd roots for allowed negative inputs. Check by differentiation.

A linear expression inside a power

\[\int k(ax+b)^n\,\mathrm{d}x= rac{k(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)}+C.\]

Require \(a e0\), \(n e-1\) and a real, defined integrand. If \(a=0\), integrate the resulting constant when it is defined. Preserve excluded inputs after algebraic cancellation.

Definite bounds

\[\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(b)-F(a),\qquad F^{\prime}=f.\]

Check the whole interval before using this directly. Constants cancel. Reverse the bounds to reverse the sign. Add adjacent integrals when they exist. A signed integral need not equal geometric area.

Improper endpoints and interior breaks

Replace an excluded or infinite bound by a valid finite bound; integrate, then take the appropriate one-sided or infinite limit. A finite limit means convergence.

Split at every interior singularity. Each one-sided contribution must converge separately. Never cancel divergences or substitute infinity as a number. A remaining tail can be found by subtracting the finite-cutoff integral from its convergent total.
revision.checks:
• New exponent, coefficient and integration constant correct?
  • Original real domain and rule exceptions checked?
  • Upper minus lower applied to the full expression?
  • Every improper contribution shown to have a finite limit?
revision.examTip: Every improper contribution shown to have a finite limit?

orig_integration_curve_equations.description: Integrate the gradient to get a family, use heights and geometric conditions to select the curve, and retain the original domain.

sections.title: Why does a gradient function describe a whole family of curves?
sections.label: The missing constant
sections.intro: Differentiation removes a constant vertical shift. On one connected interval, curves with the same derivative differ only by a constant. Knowing their slopes therefore does not tell you their heights.

blocks.html:
\[f^{\prime}(x)=g(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)=\int g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=F(x)+C.\]

The arbitrary constant describes the vertical position of the curve. A point or another independent height condition can select it.

Integrating \(f'(x)=2x\) gives the family \(f(x)=x^2+C\). At \(x=1\) all three curves have gradient \(2\). The curve through \((1,4)\) satisfies \(4=1+C\implies C=3\).

Every curve \(y=x^2+C\) has derivative \(2x\). The point \((1,4)\) selects \(C=3\).

blocks.title: Which condition chooses one member of the family?
blocks.prompt: A curve has gradient function \(f^{\prime}(x)=6x+1\), so \(f(x)=3x^2+x+C\). Which single condition below determines \(C\)? Use that condition to find its value.
blocks.hint: Both derivative conditions hold for every value of \(C\). A point supplies the missing height.
blocks.solution:
1. Use the point condition in the function:

    \[6=3(1)^2+1+C\Longrightarrow C=2.\]

  2. The gradient \(6x+1\) does not contain \(C\). Neither its value at \(2\) nor its zero can distinguish the vertically shifted curves.

blocks.html: A gradient value alone cannot determine the vertical constant. If the given derivative already fixes that gradient, the information is a check rather than a new height condition.

sections.title: How do I use a point to recover the particular curve?
sections.label: Integrate, then use the point
sections.intro: Integrate the complete gradient function and include \(+C\). Then substitute both coordinates of an allowed point into the recovered function. Do not substitute the point’s height into the derivative.

blocks.html:
If \(F^{\prime}(x)=g(x)\) and the curve passes through \((a,b)\), then

\[b=F(a)+C\Longrightarrow C=b-F(a).\]

Finish by writing the full function, not only the value of the constant.

blocks.title: Substitute a negative input into the integrated function
blocks.prompt: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=9x^2-4x+1\) and passes through \((-1,5)\). Write \(f(x)=3x^3-2x^2+x+C\). Find \(C\), then \(f(2)\).
blocks.hint: Substitute both coordinates into the recovered function, keeping brackets around the negative input.
blocks.solution:
1. \[5=3(-1)^3-2(-1)^2-1+C=-6+C\Longrightarrow C=11.\]
  2. \[f(2)=24-8+2+11=29.\]

  3. Differentiating the recovered function returns \(9x^2-4x+1\), and the given point is satisfied.

blocks.html:
1. The point \((1,4)\) fixes the position in the family \(f(x)=x^2+C\). From \(4=1+C\), obtain \(C=3\).
  2. Every curve in the family has \(f'(1)=2\). This is also the tangent gradient associated with a normal gradient of \(-\frac12\).
  3. \[y-4=2(x-1)\quad\text{(tangent)}.\]\[y-4=-\frac12(x-1)\quad\text{(normal)}.\]

For \(f(x)=x^2+3\), the statements \(f(1)=4\) and \(f^{\prime}(1)=2\) give different information: a height and a tangent gradient.
Check two things: differentiating your answer recovers the supplied gradient function, and the original point lies on the recovered curve.

sections.title: How do tangent, normal and stationary conditions supply information?
sections.label: Translate the geometry
sections.intro: Separate information about direction from information about height. A complete line equation can supply both, once its contact input is known.

blocks.html:
• A tangent gradient \(m\) at input \(a\) gives \(f^{\prime}(a)=m\).
  • A finite nonzero normal gradient \(m_N\) gives \(f^{\prime}(a)=-\frac{1}{m_N}\).
  • A point \((a,b)\) gives \(f(a)=b\).
  • A stationary point \((a,b)\) gives both \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) and \(f(a)=b\).

For a tangent line \(y=mx+q\) at input \(a\), the contact height is \(ma+q\). For a normal, use its line equation for the height and its negative reciprocal for the tangent direction.

blocks.title: Use a normal line for direction and height
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=4x+1\). The line \(x+9y=20\) is a normal at an unknown contact point. Find that point and the constant \(C\) in \(f(x)=2x^2+x+C\).
blocks.hint: The normal gradient is \(-\frac{1}{9}\), so the tangent gradient is \(9\). Use that to locate the contact input, then use the line for its height.
blocks.solution:
1. \[4a+1=9\Longrightarrow a=2.\]
  2. \[2+9y=20\Longrightarrow y=2.\]
  3. \[2=2(2)^2+2+C=10+C\Longrightarrow C=-8.\]

  4. The recovered curve passes through \((2,2)\) with tangent gradient \(9\), so its normal has the required direction and equation.

blocks.html: A vertical normal \(x=a\) means a horizontal tangent, so \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\). It supplies no height by itself. A horizontal normal requires a vertical tangent; it cannot be handled by dividing by a zero normal gradient or by assigning an ordinary finite derivative there.

When a stationary input or contact input is unknown, keep every allowed solution. A stated minimum or maximum may select a branch. If the required direction is impossible for the given derivative, changing \(C\) cannot repair it.

sections.title: What if the derivative contains an unknown coefficient?
sections.label: Linked parameters and constants
sections.intro: An unknown coefficient in the derivative and the integration constant play different roles. Keep the coefficient as a constant while integrating. Then turn every supplied height or direction into an equation and solve the equations together.

blocks.title: Two heights can determine a coefficient and the constant
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=kx+3\), where \(k\) is constant, and passes through \((0,2)\) and \((2,14)\). Find \(k\) and the integration constant \(C\).
blocks.hint: Integrate with \(k\) held constant, then substitute each point into \(f(x)=\frac{k}{2}x^2+3x+C\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[f(0)=2\Longrightarrow C=2.\]
  2. \[f(2)=2k+6+2=14\Longrightarrow k=3.\]
  3. \[f(x)=\frac{3}{2}x^2+3x+2.\]

    It satisfies both heights and has derivative \(3x+3\), as required.

blocks.html: Point conditions belong in \(f\); tangent, normal and stationary-direction conditions belong in \(f^{\prime}\). A derivative condition may determine a coefficient, while a height condition determines the vertical constant. Two distinct height conditions can also determine both.
Check all original conditions after solving. Do not assume that two statements are independent: two equivalent gradient statements still leave the vertical shift free.

sections.title: Which domain and algebraic form should the final curve keep?
sections.label: Domains and final form
sections.intro: Retain the interval supplied with the derivative and check that every used point belongs to it. Roots, denominators and cancelled factors may exclude inputs. A finite antiderivative value at an excluded endpoint does not automatically enlarge the original domain.

blocks.html: Use \(u=\sqrt{x}\) to rewrite a finished answer only after doing the calculus in \(x\). Replacing \(x\) by \(u^2\) inside an integral while leaving \(\mathrm{d}x\) unchanged is not a valid change of variable.

If the domain has separate intervals, each can have its own integration constant. A point on the left of an excluded input fixes the left constant only, unless an additional condition links the two parts. Algebraic cancellation preserves that gap.

blocks.title: One point cannot fix the constant across a domain gap
blocks.prompt: A curve is defined on \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{1\}\), with \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\) and \(f(0)=4\). On \(x<1\), write \(f(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}+x+C_L\). Find \(C_L\), then decide whether \(f(2)\) is determined.

options.no: No; the right interval has a free constant.
options.undefined: No; \(x=2\) is excluded from the domain.

blocks.hint: Cancellation preserves the exclusion at \(1\). The left and right intervals need not share an integration constant.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=x+1\quad\text{for }x\ne1.\]

  2. On the left interval, \(f(0)=C_L=4\). On the right interval, the general form is \(f(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}+x+C_R\), with \(C_R\) unrestricted by the given point.

  3. \[f(2)=4+C_R.\]

    The value exists on that interval but cannot be determined from the supplied information. The excluded input is \(1\), not \(2\).

blocks.html: A complete recovered curve includes its function equation, all determined parameter values and the original domain. If information leaves part of the family free, state which constant or component is undetermined.

glossary.definition: The derivative \(f^{\prime}(x)\), which gives the local slope at each allowed input.
Several functions sharing the same derivative on an interval but differing by a vertical constant.
A member of the family selected by sufficient additional conditions.
A statement \(f(a)=b\) fixing the height at an allowed input.
Information about a tangent, normal or stationary gradient.
Conditions that each add new information about the unknowns.
One connected interval of inputs, separated from others by excluded values.

examples.title: A point selects one vertical shift
examples.question: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x\) and passes through \((1,4)\). Find its equation.
solution: \[f(x)=\int2x\,\mathrm{d}x=x^2+C.\]

All values of \(C\) give the same derivative. The point supplies the missing height:

\[4=1^2+C\Longrightarrow C=3.\]
Its derivative is \(2x\), and \(f(1)=4\). Both original conditions are satisfied.

examples.title: Integrate before using the point coordinates
examples.question: Find the curve with gradient function \(f^{\prime}(x)=4x^3-6x+2\) that passes through \((-1,7)\).
solution:
Substitute the given input and height into this function:

\[7=(-1)^4-3(-1)^2+2(-1)+C=-4+C.\]
Differentiating gives the original gradient function. Substituting \(x=-1\) gives \(1-3-2+11=7\).

examples.title: A full normal equation can supply the missing contact point
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x-4\). The line \(x+2y=7\) is a normal at a point on the curve. Recover the curve equation.
solution:
The normal has gradient \(-\frac{1}{2}\), so the tangent gradient at the contact is \(2\).

\[2a-4=2\Longrightarrow a=3.\]

The contact point lies on the normal line:

\[3+2y=7\Longrightarrow y=2.\]
\[f(3)=9-12+C=2\Longrightarrow C=5.\]

\[f(x)=x^2-4x+5.\]

At \((3,2)\) the tangent gradient is \(2\), so the normal is \(y-2=-\frac{1}{2}(x-3)\), exactly the given line.

examples.title: A stationary height can leave more than one curve
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-12\), and one stationary point has height \(4\). Find every possible curve. Which one has a local minimum at height \(4\)?
solution: \[f(x)=x^3-12x+C,\qquad3x^2-12=0\Longrightarrow x=\pm2.\]

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x.\]

The point at \(x=-2\) is a local maximum, while the point at \(x=2\) is a local minimum.

If the stated stationary point is at \(x=-2\),

\[f(-2)=16+C=4\Longrightarrow C=-12.\]

If it is at \(x=2\),

\[f(2)=-16+C=4\Longrightarrow C=20.\]
Both \(f(x)=x^3-12x-12\) and \(f(x)=x^3-12x+20\) satisfy the stationary-height condition. The second has its local minimum at \((2,4)\).

examples.title: Keep an unknown coefficient while integrating
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=kx+2\), where \(k\) is constant, and passes through \((0,1)\) and \((2,9)\). Find its equation.
solution:
Treat \(k\) as constant when integrating with respect to \(x\):

\[f(x)=\frac{k}{2}x^2+2x+C.\]
\[f(0)=1\Longrightarrow C=1.\]
\[f(2)=2k+4+1=9\Longrightarrow k=2.\]
Its derivative is \(2x+2\), and its values at \(0\) and \(2\) are \(1\) and \(9\). The two point conditions determine both unknown constants.

examples.title: Recover the function on the stated interval before rewriting it
examples.question: For \(x>0\), a curve has \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3x-3}{\sqrt{x}}\) and passes through \((1,0)\). Find \(f(x)\), then write it as a polynomial in \(u=\sqrt{x}\). Does the recovered formula add \(x=0\) to the given domain?
solution:
First rewrite and integrate with respect to \(x\):

\[f^{\prime}(x)=3x^{\frac{1}{2}}-3x^{-\frac{1}{2}},\qquad f(x)=2x^{\frac{3}{2}}-6\sqrt{x}+C.\]
\[f(1)=2-6+C=0\Longrightarrow C=4.\]

Now use \(u=\sqrt{x}>0\) to represent the completed answer:

\[f(x)=2u^3-6u+4.\]

The expression has a finite limiting value \(4\) as \(x\) approaches zero from the right, but the specified domain is still \(x>0\). A continuous extension would be a further choice, not a consequence of integration.

extraPractice.title: A point fixes the vertical position
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has gradient \(f^{\prime}(x)=6x-4\) and passes through \((2,7)\). Write its equation as \(f(x)=Ax^2+Bx+C\) and find \(A,B,C\).
extraPractice.hint: Integrate first. Then substitute both coordinates into the recovered function, not into the gradient.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(x)=3x^2-4x+C.\]
  2. \[7=3(2)^2-4(2)+C=4+C\Longrightarrow C=3.\]
  3. \[f(x)=3x^2-4x+3.\]

  4. Its derivative is \(6x-4\), and its value at \(x=2\) is \(7\), so both conditions hold.

extraPractice.title: Recover a curve with roots and reciprocal powers
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}}-\frac{8}{x^3}\) and \(f(1)=5\). Express the curve as \(f(x)=A\sqrt{x}+\frac{B}{x^2}+C\). Find \(A,B,C\) and \(f(4)\).
extraPractice.hint: Write the gradient as \(3x^{-\frac{1}{2}}-8x^{-3}\), integrate term by term, then use the given value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(x)=6x^{\frac{1}{2}}+4x^{-2}+C.\]
  2. \[5=6+4+C\Longrightarrow C=-5.\]
  3. \[f(4)=6(2)+\frac{4}{16}-5=\frac{29}{4}.\]

  4. The original domain remains \(x>0\). Differentiation restores both terms of the supplied gradient.

extraPractice.title: Convert the normal direction before using the gradient
extraPractice.prompt: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=ax-3\), passes through \((2,1)\), and has a normal of gradient \(-\frac{1}{5}\) at that point. Find \(a\) and the integration constant \(C\) in \(f(x)=\frac{a}{2}x^2-3x+C\). Also find \(f(3)\).

retry.feedback: This uses the normal gradient as the curve gradient. First take its negative reciprocal to obtain the tangent gradient \(5\).

extraPractice.hint: The tangent gradient is the negative reciprocal of the finite nonzero normal gradient. The point condition supplies a separate equation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[m_T=-\frac{1}{-\frac{1}{5}}=5,\qquad 2a-3=5\Longrightarrow a=4.\]
  2. \[f(x)=2x^2-3x+C,\qquad1=8-6+C\Longrightarrow C=-1.\]
  3. \[f(x)=2x^2-3x-1,\qquad f(3)=18-9-1=8.\]

  4. At the contact, the derivative is \(5\), whose product with the given normal gradient is \(-1\).

extraPractice.title: A stationary point gives two conditions
extraPractice.prompt: A curve with \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x+k\) has a stationary point at \((-2,6)\). Find \(k,C\) in \(f(x)=x^2+kx+C\), and classify the stationary point.
extraPractice.hint: Use a zero derivative to determine \(k\). Use the height \(6\) only after recovering the function.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(-2)=-4+k=0\Longrightarrow k=4.\]
  2. \[f(x)=x^2+4x+C,\qquad6=4-8+C\Longrightarrow C=10.\]
  3. \[f(x)=(x+2)^2+6.\]

  4. The point is a minimum. Equivalently, \(f^{\prime\prime}=2>0\) at its stationary input.

extraPractice.title: One point need not determine both disconnected parts
extraPractice.prompt:
A differentiable function is defined on \(( -\infty,2)\cup(2,\infty)\), and

\[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2},\qquad f(0)=1.\]

Find \(f(1)\). Decide whether the supplied information determines \(f(3)\) uniquely and whether it defines \(f(2)\).

options.no: No: the right interval has an independent constant.
options.yes: Yes: one point determines every part of the domain.

options.no: No: the original domain excludes this input.

extraPractice.hint: The simplified gradient is \(x+2\), but keep \(x\ne2\). The given point belongs only to the left interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}+2x+C_-\quad(x<2),\qquad f(x)=\frac{x^2}{2}+2x+C_+\quad(x>2).\]
  2. \[f(0)=1\Longrightarrow C_-=1,\qquad f(1)=\frac{1}{2}+2+1=\frac{7}{2}.\]

  3. No condition fixes \(C_+\), so \(f(3)\) is not unique. The original domain excludes \(2\), so \(f(2)\) is not defined. An extension would require an additional condition.

starters.title: Two points determine a gradient parameter and a constant
starters.question: A curve has gradient \(f^{\prime}(x)=kx^2-6x+4\) and passes through \((1,0)\) and \((3,0)\). Find \(k\) and the constant \(C\) in its recovered equation. Then find \(m,c\) in the tangent equation \(y=mx+c\) at \((1,0)\).
starters.hint: Integrate with the parameter retained. Subtract the two point equations to eliminate the constant.
starters.solution:
1. \[f(x)=\frac{k}{3}x^3-3x^2+4x+C.\]
  2. \[0=\frac{k}{3}+1+C,\qquad0=9k-15+C.\]
  3. \[\frac{26k}{3}-16=0\Longrightarrow k=\frac{24}{13},\qquad C=-1-\frac{8}{13}=-\frac{21}{13}.\]
  4. \[f(x)=\frac{8}{13}x^3-3x^2+4x-\frac{21}{13}.\]
  5. \[m=f^{\prime}(1)=\frac{24}{13}-6+4=-\frac{2}{13}.\]
  6. \[y=-\frac{2}{13}(x-1)=-\frac{2}{13}x+\frac{2}{13}.\]

  7. Substitution gives zero at both supplied inputs, and differentiating the recovered curve returns the given parameterised gradient.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: integrate the full gradient with a constant.
  • 1 mark: form both point equations.
  • 1 mark: eliminate the constant and find the gradient parameter.
  • 1 mark: find the integration constant.
  • 1 mark: state the complete recovered curve.
  • 1 mark: obtain the tangent gradient at the specified point.
  • 1 mark: form the correct tangent equation.

starters.title: A normal line supplies both position and direction
starters.question:
For \(x>0\), a curve satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{ax+2}{\sqrt{x}}\). The normal at the point whose input is \(1\) has equation \(2x+3y=17\).

Find \(a\), recover the curve with its integration constant \(C\), and express the result using \(u=\sqrt{x}\). Find and classify the stationary point of the curve.
starters.hint: At the contact, substitute \(x=1\) into the normal line to obtain the height. Convert its gradient to the tangent gradient. Perform the calculus in \(x\), then use \(u\) to rewrite the final expression.
starters.solution:
1. \[2(1)+3y=17\Longrightarrow y=5,\qquad m_N=-\frac{2}{3},\qquad m_T=\frac{3}{2}.\]
  2. \[f^{\prime}(1)=a+2=\frac{3}{2}\Longrightarrow a=-\frac{1}{2}.\]
  3. \[f^{\prime}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x^{\frac{1}{2}}+2x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Longrightarrow f(x)=-\frac{1}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}}+4\sqrt{x}+C.\]
  4. \[5=-\frac{1}{3}+4+C\Longrightarrow C=\frac{4}{3}.\]
  5. \[u=\sqrt{x}>0:\qquad f(x)=-\frac{u^3}{3}+4u+\frac{4}{3}.\]
  6. \[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{4-x}{2\sqrt{x}}=0\Longrightarrow x=4,\qquad f(4)=\frac{20}{3}.\]

  7. The denominator is positive throughout \(x>0\). Thus the derivative is positive before \(4\) and negative after it: the stationary point is a maximum, in fact the global maximum on the stated domain.

  8. The recovered curve remains restricted to \(x>0\); the finite limit at zero does not add that input to the original curve.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: obtain the contact height from the normal line.
  • 1 mark: convert the normal gradient to the tangent gradient.
  • 1 mark: use the derivative condition to find the parameter.
  • 1 mark: integrate both gradient terms with a constant.
  • 1 mark: find the constant using the contact point.
  • 1 mark: state the complete expression in the requested representation with its domain.
  • 1 mark: find the allowed stationary input.
  • 1 mark: calculate the stationary height.
  • 1 mark: justify the classification.

revision.body:
The derivative gives direction; an independent height condition fixes the vertical position.

Recover the family and select a curve

\[f^{\prime}=g,\qquad f=F+C,\qquad F^{\prime}=g.\]\[f(a)=b\Longrightarrow C=b-F(a).\]

Integrate first, then substitute the point into the recovered function. Write the full equation and check both the derivative and the given height.

Translate geometric information

Tangent gradient \(m\): \(f^{\prime}(a)=m\). Finite nonzero normal gradient \(m_N\): \(f^{\prime}(a)=-\frac{1}{m_N}\). Use the line equation for the contact height.

A stationary point \((a,b)\) gives \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) and \(f(a)=b\). A vertical normal supplies zero tangent gradient but no height. Handle a horizontal normal as a vertical-tangent exception.

Keep linked conditions separate

Hold unknown coefficients constant while integrating. Put heights into \(f\) and directions into \(f^{\prime}\); solve for the coefficients and \(C\). Keep all valid contact inputs until a domain or nature condition selects them.

Gradient information alone cannot fix a vertical shift. Verify every original equation and any requested minimum or maximum.

Retain the domain and final form

Keep original intervals and excluded inputs, even after cancellation or when an antiderivative is finite at a boundary. Separate domain intervals may need independent constants.

After integrating in \(x\), an answer may be rewritten using \(u=\sqrt{x}\), with its corresponding domain. This is an algebraic representation, not an unchanged-variable integration step.
revision.checks:
• Whole gradient integrated with a constant?
  • Heights used in the function and directions in the derivative?
  • Every original condition and allowed branch checked?
  • Full curve and original domain stated, including any free constant?

orig_integration_areas.description: Identify the region, choose a positive strip height or width, and use the correct boundaries before integrating.

sections.title: Why can an integral be zero when the area is not?
sections.label: Signed integral or area?
sections.intro: A definite integral adds signed contributions. For increasing limits \(a<b\), a graph above the axis contributes positively and a graph below it contributes negatively. Geometric area adds the positive size of every part.

blocks.html:
\[I=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad A=\int_a^b|f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

These are equal when the graph is on or above the axis. If it is entirely on or below the axis, \(A=-I\). If its sign changes, split the region before adding areas.

Split at the crossing \(x=1\). The signed integral has cancelling contributions, while the two geometric areas add.

\[\int_0^2(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac12+\frac12=0.\]\[A=\int_0^1(1-x)\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_1^2(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=1.\]

Taking the absolute value only after the signed contributions have cancelled gives \(0\), not the geometric area.

For \(y=x-1\) on \([0,2]\), the signed contributions cancel, but the two geometric areas add to \(1\).

blocks.title: Separate the signed result from the total area
blocks.prompt: For \(f(x)=2x-1\), find the signed integral and the geometric area between the graph and the axis on \(0\le x\le2\).
blocks.hint: The root is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Calculate the two contributions separately before adding their positive areas.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\int_0^2(2x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=[x^2-x]_0^2=2.\]
  2. \[\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}}(2x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{4},\qquad\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2(2x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{9}{4}.\]
  3. \[A=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{9}{4}=\frac{5}{2}.\]

    The signed integral subtracts the part below the axis; the geometric area adds both parts.

blocks.html:
Taking the absolute value after one whole integral does not undo cancellation:

\[\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\right|\ne\int_a^b|f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x\quad\text{in general}.\]

sections.title: How do I find area above and below the axis?
sections.label: Axis crossings and signs
sections.intro: Mark the region and its outer boundaries. Solve \(f(x)=0\), retaining every allowed root inside those boundaries. Test the sign on each interval. Use \(f(x)\) where it is positive and \(-f(x)\) where it is negative, then add the results.

blocks.html: A vertical strip has height “top minus bottom”. For the axis and a graph, that height is either \(f(x)-0\) or \(0-f(x)\). It must be nonnegative throughout the interval being integrated.

blocks.title: Keep the area positive when the graph is below the axis
blocks.prompt: Find the area between \(y=2x-6\), the axis and the vertical lines \(x=0\) and \(x=2\).
blocks.hint: The graph is below the axis throughout this interval. The vertical gap is \(0-(2x-6)\).
blocks.solution:
1. At the endpoints the heights are \(-6\) and \(-2\); this straight line stays below the axis between them.

  2. \[A=\int_0^2(6-2x)\,\mathrm{d}x=[6x-x^2]_0^2=8.\]

blocks.html: A root may be a touch rather than a crossing. Do not change the sign of the integrand automatically at every root; check the sign on both sides.

If a region reaches an undefined input or extends without bound, use the improper-integral limits from the earlier lesson. Each nonnegative area piece must converge. Ordinary endpoint substitution cannot justify a finite area across a singularity.

sections.title: How do I find the area between two graphs?
sections.label: Upper minus lower
sections.intro: Solve the original intersection equation \(f(x)=g(x)\). Check any roots introduced by squaring or clearing a denominator against the original graphs and their domains. A region enclosed only by two graphs has intersection boundaries; supplied vertical lines may give different outer limits.

blocks.html:
\[A=\int_a^b\bigl(\text{upper function}-\text{lower function}\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

Choose the order using a sketch or a test input between intersections. If the graphs change order, split the region and reverse the subtraction on the affected part.

blocks.title: Find the intersections and then the vertical gap
blocks.prompt: Find the intersection inputs and the enclosed area between \(y=3-x^2\) and \(y=x^2+1\).
blocks.hint: Solve the intersection equation, then test which graph is higher between the two inputs.
blocks.solution:
1. \[3-x^2=x^2+1\Longrightarrow x^2=1\Longrightarrow x=-1\text{ or }x=1.\]

  2. The graph \(3-x^2\) is higher on \(-1<x<1\), so the vertical gap is \(2-2x^2\).

  3. \[A=\int_{-1}^1(2-2x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[2x-\frac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^1=\frac{8}{3}.\]

blocks.html: Show the intersection equation, the correct bounds and the gap in each integral. A calculator can check the arithmetic; the displayed setup explains which region you found.
The signs of the two heights do not decide which graph is upper. Compare their actual values. If both axes measure lengths in the same unit, report the area in the corresponding square unit.

sections.title: When should I use horizontal strips?
sections.label: Right minus left
sections.intro: Choose horizontal strips when the boundaries are easier to write as \(x\) in terms of \(y\). Each strip is a thin rectangle: its width is the right coordinate minus the left coordinate, and its thickness is \(\mathrm{d}y\).

blocks.html:
\[A=\int_c^d\bigl(x_{\text{right}}(y)-x_{\text{left}}(y)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]

Use limits in \(y\). Keep the inverse branches that describe the actual region, and split at any height where its left or right boundary changes.

The first-quadrant region between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\) can be sliced either way.

\[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac43\quad\text{(vertical strips)}.\]\[A=\int_0^4\left(\sqrt y-\frac y2\right)\,\mathrm{d}y=\frac43\quad\text{(horizontal strips)}.\]

The same first-quadrant region has vertical gap \(2x-x^2\) and horizontal gap \(\sqrt{y}-\frac{y}{2}\). The corresponding limits are \(0\le x\le2\) and \(0\le y\le4\).

blocks.title: Use right minus left with limits in the same variable
blocks.prompt: The curves \(x=y^2\) and \(x=3y\) enclose a region. Find the lower and upper limits in \(y\), then its area using horizontal strips.
blocks.hint: Solve \(y^2=3y\). Between these values, compare the horizontal positions \(y^2\) and \(3y\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[y^2=3y\Longrightarrow y=0\text{ or }y=3.\]

  2. For \(0<y<3\), the right boundary is \(x=3y\), and the left boundary is \(x=y^2\).

  3. \[A=\int_0^3(3y-y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y=\left[\frac{3y^2}{2}-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^3=\frac{9}{2}.\]

blocks.html: Changing the differential from \(\mathrm{d}x\) to \(\mathrm{d}y\) also changes the functions and limits. Reusing the old input bounds gives a different calculation.

sections.title: How do I find an unknown boundary?
sections.label: Form and check an area equation
sections.intro: First decide where the unknown boundary lies relative to roots and intersections. Use the given position to form the correct sum of positive areas. Equate that expression to the stated area and solve.

blocks.title: Filter the roots using the stated position of the boundary
blocks.prompt: The geometric area between \(y=x-2\), the axis and the vertical lines \(x=0\) and \(x=b\) is \(4\) square units, where \(b>2\). Find both roots of the resulting quadratic equation, then the valid value of \(b\).
blocks.hint: The fixed part below the axis has area \(2\). The part to the right of the root has area \(\frac{(b-2)^2}{2}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[2+\frac{(b-2)^2}{2}=4\Longrightarrow(b-2)^2=4.\]
  2. \[b=0\text{ or }b=4.\]

  3. Only \(b=4\) satisfies \(b>2\), the condition used to form this area expression. It gives area \(2+2=4\). The other algebraic root does not describe the stated region.

blocks.html: Keep every algebraic solution until you check it against the original domain, boundary direction and interval used in the area formula. Substitute each remaining solution into the original area expression.
If the boundary position is not specified, consider its possible intervals separately. A formula derived for a boundary to the right of a crossing cannot be used unchanged to its left.

glossary.definition: A total that adds contributions above the axis and subtracts contributions below it, for increasing limits.
The nonnegative size of a region; separate pieces are added without cancellation.
A curve, axis or line forming an edge of the required region.
A point belonging to both bounding graphs.
A thin rectangle with height equal to the upper function minus the lower function, integrated in \(x\).
A thin rectangle with width equal to the right coordinate minus the left coordinate, integrated in \(y\).
The part of an inverted equation that describes the boundary in the required region.

examples.title: Equal signed contributions can cancel
examples.question: For \(y=x-1\), calculate the signed integral and the total area between the graph and the axis on \(0\le x\le2\).
solution: \[I=\int_0^2(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-x\right]_0^2=0.\]

The root is \(x=1\). The graph is below the axis before this root and above it afterwards.

\[\int_0^1(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=-\frac{1}{2},\qquad\int_1^2(x-1)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}.\]

For geometric area, add the positive sizes of the two regions:

\[A=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1.\]
The integral is zero because the signed contributions cancel. The total area is one square unit.

examples.title: A touching root does not force a change of sign
examples.question: Find the area between \(y=-(x+1)^2\), the axis and the vertical lines \(x=-2\) and \(x=1\).
solution: Since \(-(x+1)^2\le0\), the whole graph lies on or below the axis. It touches the axis at \(x=-1\) and stays below on both sides.

The positive vertical gap is \(0-[-(x+1)^2]=(x+1)^2\). One integral is sufficient:

\[A=\int_{-2}^1(x+1)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
The area is three square units. Splitting at the touching root would give the same result, with no change in the gap formula.

examples.title: Find an enclosed area using vertical strips
examples.question: Find the area enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\).
solution:
Find the intersection inputs:

\[x^2=2x\Longrightarrow x(x-2)=0\Longrightarrow x=0\text{ or }x=2.\]
On \(0<x<2\), the line is higher than the parabola. The vertical strip has height \(2x-x^2\).
The enclosed area is \(\frac{4}{3}\) square units.

examples.title: Both graphs lie below the axis and change order
examples.question: Find the area between \(f(x)=x^2-6\), \(g(x)=-x^2-4\) and the supplied vertical boundaries \(x=-2\), \(x=2\).
solution:
Both graphs lie below the axis on this interval. Their relative heights determine the gap:

\[f(x)-g(x)=2x^2-2=0\Longrightarrow x=\pm1.\]
The function \(f\) is higher on the two outer intervals; \(g\) is higher on the middle interval. Keep the supplied outer boundaries.
\[\begin{aligned}A={}&\int_{-2}^{-1}(2x^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&+\int_{-1}^{1}(2-2x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\\&+\int_{1}^{2}(2x^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}x.\end{aligned}\]

The outer pieces are equal by symmetry. For the right one,

\[\int_1^2(2x^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{2x^3}{3}-2x\right]_1^2=\frac{8}{3}.\]

\[A=\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{3}+\frac{8}{3}=8.\]

Each piece is positive even though both bounding graphs have negative heights.

examples.title: Describe the same region with horizontal strips
examples.question: Find the area enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\) again, this time integrating with respect to \(y\).
solution: The intersections are \((0,0)\) and \((2,4)\), so the limits in \(y\) are \(0\) and \(4\).
The region is in the first quadrant. Inverting the parabola uses its positive branch \(x=\sqrt{y}\); the line becomes \(x=\frac{y}{2}\).

For \(0<y<4\), the parabola is the right boundary and the line is the left boundary. Therefore,

\[A=\int_0^4\left(\sqrt{y}-\frac{y}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]
The two strip directions give the same area. The functions, limits and differential all use the chosen variable.

examples.title: An area equation can produce an invalid boundary
examples.question: The geometric area between \(y=x-1\), the axis and the vertical lines \(x=0\), \(x=b\) is \(5\) square units, where \(b>1\). Find \(b\).
solution: The part from \(0\) to \(1\) lies below the axis and has area \(\frac{1}{2}\). Because \(b>1\), the remaining part lies above it.
\[\frac{1}{2}+\frac{(b-1)^2}{2}=5\Longrightarrow(b-1)^2=9\Longrightarrow b=4\text{ or }b=-2.\]
Reject \(b=-2\): it fails \(b>1\), so it does not belong to the region used in this equation.

\[b=4,\qquad A=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{9}{2}=5.\]

Checking the original area confirms the valid boundary.
