extraPractice.title: Cancellation changes the integral but not the geometric area
extraPractice.prompt: For \(y=x-2\) on \(0\le x\le5\), find the signed integral \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^5(x-2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) and the total geometric area \(A\) between the graph and the horizontal axis over that interval.

retry.feedback: This is the net integral. Add the magnitudes of the pieces on the two sides of \(x=2\).

extraPractice.hint: The graph crosses the axis at \(x=2\). The part below the axis has positive geometric area but a negative signed contribution.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[I=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}-2x\right]_0^5=\frac{5}{2}.\]
  2. \[A=-\int_0^2(x-2)\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_2^5(x-2)\,\mathrm{d}x=2+\frac{9}{2}=\frac{13}{2}.\]

  3. The geometric area is the sum of two positive pieces. Taking the absolute value of the net integral would still miss some area.

extraPractice.title: A touching root does not force a sign reversal
extraPractice.prompt: Find the geometric area between \(y=(x-1)^2(x+2)\), the horizontal axis and the vertical lines \(x=-2\) and \(x=2\). Does the graph change sign at \(x=1\)?

fields.label: Sign change at the touching root?

options.no: No: the squared factor remains nonnegative.
options.yes: Yes: every root reverses the sign.

extraPractice.hint: On the stated interval, \(x+2\ge0\) and \((x-1)^2\ge0\). Check the sign before deciding to reverse any integral.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(x-1)^2(x+2)=x^3-3x+2\ge0\qquad(-2\le x\le2).\]
  2. \[A=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-\frac{3x^2}{2}+2x\right]_{-2}^{2}=2-(-6)=8.\]

  3. The function is positive on both sides of \(1\) within this interval and zero at \(1\). It touches the axis without changing sign. Splitting there is optional; neither part needs a negative sign.

extraPractice.title: Find intersections before choosing the area limits
extraPractice.prompt: Find the intersection points of \(y=x^2\) and \(y=x+2\), then find the area enclosed by the two graphs.
extraPractice.hint: Set the two heights equal. Between the intersection inputs, determine which graph is higher.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x^2=x+2\Longleftrightarrow(x-2)(x+1)=0.\]

  2. The intersections are \((-1,1)\) and \((2,4)\). On the interval between them, the line is above the parabola.

  3. \[A=\int_{-1}^{2}(x+2-x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}+2x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}.\]
  4. \[A=\frac{10}{3}-\left(-\frac{7}{6}\right)=\frac{9}{2}.\]

extraPractice.title: Upper minus lower also works below the axis
extraPractice.prompt: The graphs \(y=x^2-5\) and \(y=-4\) enclose a region below the horizontal axis. Which graph is the upper boundary between their intersections, and what is the area?
extraPractice.hint: The vertical strip height is a difference of heights. It is positive even when both heights are negative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x^2-5=-4\Longrightarrow x=-1,1.\]

  2. Between these inputs, the line has height \(-4\), while the curve is at or below \(-4\). Thus the line is the upper boundary.

  3. \[A=\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl[-4-(x^2-5)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{4}{3}.\]

extraPractice.title: A horizontal strip uses horizontal distances
extraPractice.prompt: A region is enclosed by \(x=y^2\) and \(x=2y+3\). Use horizontal strips to find the lower and upper \(y\)-limits and the enclosed area.
extraPractice.hint: Solve for the intersection values of \(y\). Subtract the left-hand \(x\)-value from the right-hand \(x\)-value.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[y^2=2y+3\Longleftrightarrow(y-3)(y+1)=0\Longrightarrow y=-1,3.\]

  2. For \(-1\le y\le3\), the line is the right boundary and the parabola is the left boundary.

  3. \[A=\int_{-1}^{3}(2y+3-y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y=\left[y^2+3y-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{3}.\]
  4. \[A=9-\left(-\frac{5}{3}\right)=\frac{32}{3}.\]

  5. The limits and differential both use \(y\). Using intersection \(x\)-coordinates as these limits would describe a different calculation.

starters.title: Two enclosed pieces require a change of upper boundary
starters.question: The curves \(y=x^3-x\) and \(y=x\) enclose two bounded regions. Find all their intersection points, each separate area and the total enclosed area. Also evaluate the signed difference integral from the leftmost intersection input to the rightmost.
starters.hint: Factor the height difference \(x^3-2x\) and test its sign on each interval. The same subtraction order cannot give positive strip heights on both sides of zero.
starters.solution:
1. \[x^3-x=x\Longleftrightarrow x(x^2-2)=0\Longrightarrow x=-\sqrt{2},0,\sqrt{2}.\]

  2. Since \(y=x\) at every intersection, the points are \((-\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2})\), \((0,0)\) and \((\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})\).

  3. The cubic is above the line on \((-\sqrt{2},0)\), and the line is above the cubic on \((0,\sqrt{2})\).

  4. \[A_L=\int_{-\sqrt{2}}^0(x^3-2x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{x^4}{4}-x^2\right]_{-\sqrt{2}}^0=1.\]
  5. \[A_R=\int_0^{\sqrt{2}}(2x-x^3)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[x^2-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^{\sqrt{2}}=1.\]
  6. \[A=A_L+A_R=2,\qquad\int_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(x^3-2x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1-1=0.\]

  7. The zero signed result represents cancellation of equal contributions; it does not mean that no region is enclosed.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: solve the complete intersection equation.
  • 1 mark: state all intersection coordinates.
  • 1 mark: establish the upper boundary on each interval.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the left area using positive strip height.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the right area using positive strip height.
  • 1 mark: obtain the total geometric area.
  • 1 mark: distinguish the signed difference integral from the geometric total.

starters.title: An area condition selects the correct endpoint
starters.question:
The total geometric area between \(y=x-3\), the horizontal axis and the vertical lines \(x=1\) and \(x=b\) is \(10\), where \(b>3\).

Find \(b\), the separate areas below and above the axis, and the signed integral \(I=\displaystyle\int_1^b(x-3)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
starters.hint: The crossing is at \(x=3\). The first geometric area is fixed; the second depends on the unknown endpoint. Apply \(b>3\) after solving the area equation.
starters.solution:
1. \[A_-=-\int_1^3(x-3)\,\mathrm{d}x=2.\]
  2. \[A_+=\int_3^b(x-3)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{(b-3)^2}{2}\qquad(b>3).\]
  3. \[2+\frac{(b-3)^2}{2}=10\Longrightarrow(b-3)^2=16\Longrightarrow b=7\ \text{or}\ b=-1.\]

  4. The required endpoint satisfies \(b>3\), so only \(b=7\) belongs to this region. The other algebraic root is rejected.

  5. \[A_-=2,\qquad A_+=8,\qquad I=-A_-+A_+=6.\]

  6. The geometric total is \(2+8=10\), while the signed integral subtracts the below-axis contribution.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: identify the sign-changing input and split the region.
  • 1 mark: calculate the fixed below-axis area.
  • 1 mark: express the variable above-axis area using the unknown endpoint.
  • 1 mark: form and solve the total-area equation.
  • 1 mark: apply the endpoint restriction and select the valid root.
  • 1 mark: state the separate geometric areas.
  • 1 mark: calculate the signed integral with the correct signs.

revision.body:
Choose the region and a positive gap before calculating its integral.

Signed integral versus geometric area

\[I=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad A=\int_a^b|f(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

For \(a<b\), contributions below the axis are negative in \(I\). Split where the sign changes and add positive pieces for area. Taking the modulus of the whole signed integral can hide cancellation. A touching root need not change the sign.

Vertical strips: upper minus lower

\[A=\int_a^b(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

Solve the original intersection equation and check its roots. Keep supplied outer boundaries. Test the order between intersections and split where it changes. The rule also works when both graphs lie below the axis.

Horizontal strips: right minus left

\[A=\int_c^d(\text{right}-\text{left})\,\mathrm{d}y.\]

Write the boundaries as \(x\) in terms of \(y\), using the correct branches. Use limits in \(y\) and split where a boundary changes. Choose the orientation that describes the region most clearly.

Unknown bounds and final checks

Form an equation for the total positive area. Check every algebraic root against the stated domain, boundary position and branch of the formula. If the position is unknown, consider separate intervals.

Verify nonnegative pieces and the requested region. Use square units for a geometric length model. At singular or infinite boundaries, each required improper area integral must converge.
revision.checks:
• Region and all relevant crossings identified?
  • Positive gap and correct variable used on each piece?
  • Original domains and supplied boundaries retained?
  • Every boundary solution checked in the original area?
revision.examTip: Every boundary solution checked in the original area?

orig_integration_volumes.description: Choose a perpendicular cross-section, measure its radii from the axis, and integrate its area without counting any part twice.

sections.title: How does rotating a region create a volume?
sections.label: Disks and distances
sections.intro: A solid of revolution is the three-dimensional region swept out by one complete turn about an axis. Cut it perpendicular to that axis. When the original strip runs from the axis to a curve, the cross-section is a filled disk.

blocks.html:
A disk of radius \(R\) has area \(\pi R^2\). Adding thin disk volumes about the \(x\)-axis gives

\[V=\pi\int_a^b R(x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

For the region between \(y=f(x)\) and that axis, \(R=|f(x)|\), so \(R^2=f(x)^2\). Square the function before integrating.

blocks.title: Square the radius before integrating
blocks.prompt: The region bounded by \(y=\sqrt{3x+2}\), the \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x=0\), \(x=2\) is rotated through one complete turn about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.
blocks.hint: The cross-section is a disk. Its squared radius is \(y^2=3x+2\).

blocks.html: The radius is a nonnegative distance from the rotation axis. A negative coordinate is not a negative radius. Also, integrating the radius itself finds neither the disk area nor the volume.

sections.title: How do I calculate a volume with a hole?
sections.label: Outer disk minus inner disk
sections.intro: If the perpendicular strip stays on one side of the axis without reaching it, its rotation leaves a central hole. The cross-section is a washer: an outer disk with an inner disk removed.

blocks.html:
\[A=\pi R^2-\pi r^2=\pi(R^2-r^2),\qquad0\le r\le R.\]\[V=\pi\int_a^b\bigl(R(x)^2-r(x)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

Measure both radii from the axis. The farther boundary supplies \(R\), and the nearer one supplies \(r\). Find intersections where needed, and retain any supplied end boundaries.

At \(x=1\), the two radii measured from the rotation axis are \(R=2x=2\) and \(r=x^2=1\).

\[A=\pi(R^2-r^2)=4\pi-\pi=3\pi.\]

Square each radius before subtracting. Using \(\pi(R-r)^2\) would give \(\pi\). If \(r=0\), the cross-section is a full disc.

At \(x=1\) in the region between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\), the radii are \(2\) and \(1\). The washer area is \(3\pi\), not \(\pi\).

blocks.title: Subtract squared radii, not the squared gap
blocks.prompt: The region between \(y=x+1\), \(y=1\), \(x=0\) and \(x=2\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.
blocks.hint: The outer radius is \(x+1\), and the inner radius is \(1\). Expand \((x+1)^2-1^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[R=x+1,\qquad r=1,\qquad R^2-r^2=x^2+2x.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\int_0^2(x^2+2x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+x^2\right]_0^2=\frac{20\pi}{3}.\]

  3. Using \([(x+1)-1]^2=x^2\) would square the gap between the graphs instead of subtracting the disk areas.

blocks.html:
\[R^2-r^2\ne(R-r)^2\quad\text{in general}.\]

Subtract the two disk areas; do not square the gap between the graphs. Below the axis, the lower graph may be the farther boundary.

sections.title: What changes when I rotate about the y-axis?
sections.label: Horizontal radii and limits
sections.intro: For disks or washers about the \(y\)-axis, use horizontal strips and integrate with respect to \(y\). Rewrite each required boundary as \(x\) in terms of \(y\), keeping the branch that belongs to the region.

blocks.html:
\[V=\pi\int_c^d\bigl(R(y)^2-r(y)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]

The radii are horizontal distances from the \(y\)-axis, and \(c,d\) are limits in \(y\). For an axis-to-curve region, set \(r=0\) and use \(R=|x(y)|\).

For the region between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\), each washer is perpendicular to the axis of rotation.

\[V_x=\pi\int_0^2\big[(2x)^2-(x^2)^2\big]\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{64\pi}{15}.\]\[V_y=\pi\int_0^4\left[(\sqrt y)^2-\left(\frac y2\right)^2\right]\,\mathrm{d}y=\frac{8\pi}{3}.\]

The same region between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\) produces different washers about the two axes. Match the radii, limits and differential to the chosen axis.

blocks.title: Use horizontal disks about the vertical axis
blocks.prompt: The region \(0\le x\le\sqrt{2y+1}\), \(0\le y\le3\), is rotated about the \(y\)-axis. Find the exact volume.
blocks.hint: The radius is a horizontal distance. Use \(x^2=2y+1\) and integrate with respect to \(y\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^3(2y+1)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]
  2. \[V=\pi[y^2+y]_0^3=12\pi.\]

  3. The limits \(0\) and \(3\) are heights in \(y\), matching \(\mathrm{d}y\).

blocks.html: Write the axis first, then a typical cross-section, its radii and its limits. Rearranging a boundary and squaring its radius are separate steps; do both explicitly when the algebra is easy to confuse.

sections.title: When must I split the solid into separate parts?
sections.label: Changing radii and filled disks
sections.intro: Inspect the perpendicular strip as it moves through the region. Split where a boundary changes, where a hole starts or ends, or where a different boundary becomes farther from the axis. Axis crossings and equal-distance equations can give different split points.

blocks.html:
For a vertical strip \(L(x)\le y\le U(x)\) that contains the \(x\)-axis,

\[r=0,\qquad R=\max\bigl(|L(x)|,|U(x)|\bigr).\]

It produces one filled disk. If both endpoints are on the same side, use the larger distance as \(R\) and the smaller as \(r\). Apply the same distance reasoning to horizontal strips about the \(y\)-axis.

blocks.title: A strip crossing the axis produces one disk
blocks.prompt: The rectangle \(0\le x\le2\), \(-1\le y\le3\), is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find its outer and inner radii, then its volume.
blocks.hint: The vertical segment contains the axis. Its rotation fills a disk out to the larger distance from the axis.
blocks.solution:
1. \[R=\max(1,3)=3,\qquad r=0.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\int_0^2 3^2\,\mathrm{d}x=18\pi.\]

  3. The rotation of the lower part is already contained in the rotation of the upper part. Adding both disk volumes would count some material twice; subtracting them would create a hole that is not present.

blocks.html: Rotating the parts above and below an axis separately can produce overlapping disks. Adding their volumes counts that overlap twice. Determine the cross-section of the whole rotated strip first.

sections.title: How do I use a volume model to find an unknown?
sections.label: Capacity, parameters and checks
sections.intro: Identify what the model measures: interior capacity, total enclosed volume or the material between two surfaces. Form the appropriate disk or washer integral, then use the stated volume to solve for an unknown height or scale.

blocks.title: Choose the physically allowed radial scale
blocks.prompt: Coordinates are measured in centimetres. A container’s interior is formed by rotating \(0\le x\le k\sqrt{y}\), \(0\le y\le4\), about the \(y\)-axis, where \(k>0\). Its capacity is \(32\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^3\). Find both roots of the equation for \(k\), then the allowed value.
blocks.hint: Use the squared radius \(k^2y\). The positive-scale condition must still be applied after solving.
blocks.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^4k^2y\,\mathrm{d}y=8\pi k^2.\]
  2. \[8\pi k^2=32\pi\Longrightarrow k^2=4\Longrightarrow k=\pm2.\]

  3. The model requires \(k>0\), so \(k=2\). This gives the stated capacity and a nonnegative radial boundary on the full height interval.

blocks.html: Retain every algebraic root until the physical restrictions and original domain are checked. Heights and radial scales may be required to be positive. Verify that the selected boundaries remain real and correctly ordered over the whole interval.

Use consistent length units before integrating. The result is in cubic units; for capacity, \(1000\,\mathrm{cm}^3=1\,\mathrm{L}\). Keep \(\pi\) exact unless a rounded answer is requested. If a boundary is infinite or singular, test convergence of the radius-squared volume integral using limits.

State the final physical quantity with its unit and substitute it back into the original volume model. For a hollow object, subtract the interior volume only over the interval where that cavity exists.

glossary.definition: The three-dimensional region swept out when a plane region makes one complete turn about an axis.
The shape obtained by cutting the solid with a plane; here the cut is perpendicular to the rotation axis.
A filled circular cross-section with no central hole.
A circular cross-section with an inner disk removed.
The greatest distance from the rotation axis reached by the cross-section.
The radius of the central hole; zero for a filled disk.
The volume available inside a container.

examples.title: A graph below the axis still gives a positive radius
examples.question: The region between \(y=-\sqrt{2x+1}\), the \(x\)-axis and the lines \(x=0\), \(x=4\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find its volume.
solution:
A perpendicular cross-section is a disk. Its radius is the distance from the axis:

\[R=|y|=\sqrt{2x+1}.\]
\[R^2=2x+1,\qquad V=\pi\int_0^4(2x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
The volume is \(20\pi\) cubic units. A negative graph height does not give a negative radius or volume.

examples.title: Rotate an enclosed region to form washers
examples.question: The region enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.
solution: \[x^2=2x\Longrightarrow x=0\text{ or }x=2.\]

On \(0<x<2\), both graphs are above the axis. The farther boundary is \(y=2x\), so

\[R=2x,\qquad r=x^2.\]

Subtract the inner disk area from the outer disk area at each input:

\[V=\pi\int_0^2\bigl[(2x)^2-(x^2)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
\[V=\pi\left[\frac{4x^3}{3}-\frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2=\pi\left(\frac{32}{3}-\frac{32}{5}\right)=\frac{64\pi}{15}.\]

examples.title: The lower graph can be the outer boundary
examples.question: The region between \(y=-x\), \(y=-2x\), \(x=1\) and \(x=3\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find its volume.
solution:
Both graphs lie below the axis. The graph \(y=-2x\) is farther from the axis, although its height is lower:

\[R=2x,\qquad r=x.\]
\[V=\pi\int_1^3\bigl[(2x)^2-x^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x=3\pi\int_1^3x^2\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
Comparing distances, rather than calling the higher graph the outer one, gives a nonnegative cross-sectional area throughout.

examples.title: Rotate the same enclosed region about the other axis
examples.question: Rotate the region enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x\) about the \(y\)-axis. Find the volume and compare it with the rotation about the \(x\)-axis.
solution: The intersection points are \((0,0)\) and \((2,4)\). Horizontal cross-sections therefore use \(0\le y\le4\).

In this first-quadrant region, the right boundary is \(x=\sqrt{y}\), using the positive branch. The left boundary is \(x=\frac{y}{2}\). Thus

\[R=\sqrt{y},\qquad r=\frac{y}{2}.\]
\[V=\pi\int_0^4\left(y-\frac{y^2}{4}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]
\[V=\pi\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{y^3}{12}\right]_0^4=\pi\left(8-\frac{16}{3}\right)=\frac{8\pi}{3}.\]
The original region is unchanged, but the rotation axis changes the cross-sections. Its two volumes are \(\frac{64\pi}{15}\) about the \(x\)-axis and \(\frac{8\pi}{3}\) about the \(y\)-axis.

examples.title: The outer radius and the presence of a hole can both change
examples.question: Rotate the region between \(y=x-2\), \(y=1\) and the vertical lines \(x=0\), \(x=3\) about the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.
solution:
For \(0\le x\le2\), the vertical segment reaches across the axis. It rotates into one filled disk. Compare its boundary distances:

\[2-x=1\Longrightarrow x=1.\]
Beyond \(x=2\), the lower boundary is positive, so the slice has a central hole. Use \(R=1\) and \(r=x-2\) for the final interval.
\[\begin{aligned}V=\pi\biggl(&\int_0^1(2-x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x+\int_1^2 1\,\mathrm{d}x\\&+\int_2^3\bigl[1-(x-2)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x\biggr).\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}\int_0^1(2-x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x&=\frac{7}{3},\\\int_1^2 1\,\mathrm{d}x&=1,\\\int_2^3\bigl[1-(x-2)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x&=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\]

\[V=\pi\left(\frac{7}{3}+1+\frac{2}{3}\right)=4\pi.\]

Each slice of the solid is included exactly once.

examples.title: Use a capacity to recover the allowed height
examples.question: Coordinates are measured in centimetres. A container’s interior is formed by rotating \(0\le x\le\sqrt{3y+4}\), \(0\le y\le h\), about the \(y\)-axis, where \(h>0\). Its capacity is \(14\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^3\). Find \(h\).
solution:
The squared interior radius is \(3y+4\), so its capacity is

\[V=\pi\int_0^h(3y+4)\,\mathrm{d}y=\pi\left(\frac{3h^2}{2}+4h\right).\]
\[\frac{3h^2}{2}+4h=14\Longrightarrow3h^2+8h-28=0.\]
\[(h-2)(3h+14)=0\Longrightarrow h=2\text{ or }h=-\frac{14}{3}.\]
Only the positive height is allowed, so \(h=2\,\mathrm{cm}\). The radial expression is real and positive throughout \(0\le y\le2\).

\[V=\pi\left(\frac{3(2)^2}{2}+4(2)\right)=14\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^3.\]

This checks the capacity in the original model.

extraPractice.title: Square the radius before integrating
extraPractice.prompt: The region between \(y=\sqrt{3x+1}\), the horizontal axis, \(x=0\) and \(x=2\) is rotated fully about the horizontal axis. Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the volume.
extraPractice.hint: The radius is \(\sqrt{3x+1}\), so the circular cross-section has area \(\pi(3x+1)\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^2\left(\sqrt{3x+1}\right)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\int_0^2(3x+1)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\left[\frac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_0^2=8\pi\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  3. The integration variable measures distance along the rotation axis; the final units are cubic.

extraPractice.title: A negative height still gives a positive radius
extraPractice.prompt: The region between \(y=-2x\), the horizontal axis and the lines \(x=1\) and \(x=3\) is rotated about the horizontal axis. Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the volume.
extraPractice.hint: The radius is the distance from the curve to the axis: \(|-2x|=2x\) on this interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[R=2x,\qquad V=\pi\int_1^3(2x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
  2. \[V=4\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_1^3=\frac{104\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  3. The rotated region has disks, with no inner hole. A negative curve height does not make the volume negative.

extraPractice.title: Subtract the hole from every cross-section
extraPractice.prompt: The region between \(y=4\), \(y=x+1\), \(x=0\) and \(x=2\) is rotated about the horizontal axis. Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the volume.

retry.feedback: This squares the radial gap. A washer needs \(\pi(R^2-r^2)\), not \(\pi(R-r)^2\).
This is the outer cylinder. Subtract the volume of the inner hole.

extraPractice.hint: The outer radius is \(4\), and the inner radius is \(x+1\). The washer area uses the difference of their squares.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^2\bigl[16-(x+1)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\left[16x-\frac{(x+1)^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\pi\left(32-\frac{26}{3}\right)=\frac{70\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  3. The inner radius remains smaller than the outer radius over the whole interval. Squaring the thickness \(4-(x+1)\) would calculate a different disk.

extraPractice.title: Use horizontal disks about the vertical axis
extraPractice.prompt: The region between \(x=y^2+1\), the vertical axis, \(y=0\) and \(y=1\) is rotated about the vertical axis. Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the volume.

retry.feedback: The squared radius still needs the circle-area factor \(\pi\).

extraPractice.hint: The radius is already written as a function of \(y\). Square the entire expression and integrate with respect to \(y\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^1(y^2+1)^2\,\mathrm{d}y=\pi\int_0^1(y^4+2y^2+1)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\left[\frac{y^5}{5}+\frac{2y^3}{3}+y\right]_0^1=\frac{28\pi}{15}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  3. These are \(y\)-limits and horizontal cross-sections. No extra change of variable is needed.

extraPractice.title: One region creates different volumes about different axes
extraPractice.prompt: The graphs \(y=x^2\) and \(y=3x\) enclose a first-quadrant region. Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the volume obtained by rotating this region about each coordinate axis separately.
extraPractice.hint: For the horizontal axis, compare the two heights. For the vertical axis, rewrite both boundaries in terms of \(y\), choosing the positive square-root branch.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x^2=3x\Longrightarrow x=0,3,\qquad y=0,9.\]
  2. \[V_x=\pi\int_0^3\bigl[(3x)^2-(x^2)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left[3x^3-\frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^3=\frac{162\pi}{5}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  3. For horizontal strips, the right boundary is \(x=\sqrt{y}\), and the left boundary is \(x=\frac{y}{3}\). These are the outer and inner distances from the vertical axis.

  4. \[V_y=\pi\int_0^9\left[y-\frac{y^2}{9}\right]\,\mathrm{d}y=\pi\left[\frac{y^2}{2}-\frac{y^3}{27}\right]_0^9=\frac{27\pi}{2}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  5. Changing the axis changes the cross-sections, radii and limits. The two volumes need not agree.

starters.title: A strip crossing the axis must not be counted twice
starters.question:
The region between \(y=x-2\), \(y=x+1\), \(x=0\) and \(x=3\) is rotated fully about the horizontal axis. Coordinates are in centimetres.

Find the input where the outer radius changes from the lower boundary to the upper boundary, the boundary input beyond which an inner hole appears, and the total volume. Show the cross-sectional formula on each interval.
starters.hint: While the strip contains the axis, rotation makes one complete disk with the larger absolute endpoint distance as its radius. A washer appears only once both endpoints are on the same side of the axis.
starters.solution:
1. For \(0\le x\le2\), the strip reaches from \(x-2\le0\) to \(x+1>0\), so it crosses or touches the axis. Its outer distance is the larger of \(2-x\) and \(x+1\).

  2. \[2-x=x+1\Longrightarrow x=\frac{1}{2}.\]

  3. On \(0\le x\le\frac{1}{2}\), the disk radius is \(2-x\). On \(\frac{1}{2}\le x\le2\), the disk radius is \(x+1\). For \(2<x\le3\), the washer has outer radius \(x+1\) and inner radius \(x-2\).

  4. \[\begin{aligned}\frac{V}{\pi}&=\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}}(2-x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\\&\quad+\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2(x+1)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\\&\quad+\int_2^3\bigl[(x+1)^2-(x-2)^2\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}x.\end{aligned}\]
  5. \[V=\pi\left(\frac{37}{24}+\frac{63}{8}+12\right)=\frac{257\pi}{12}\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  6. At the transition \(x=2\), the inner radius is zero; it becomes positive immediately to the right. Adding the separate rotations above and below the axis would count their overlapping disks twice.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: recognise that a strip crossing the axis gives one disk.
  • 1 mark: find the change in outer-radius boundary.
  • 1 mark: find where the inner hole starts.
  • 1 mark: form the first disk integral.
  • 1 mark: form the second disk integral.
  • 1 mark: form the washer integral.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the separate nonnegative contributions.
  • 1 mark: give the total volume with cubic units.

starters.title: Use a volume condition to recover a physical length
starters.question:
A solid is formed by rotating the region between \(y=\sqrt{4x+9}\), the horizontal axis, \(x=0\) and \(x=h\) about the horizontal axis. Coordinates are in centimetres, \(h>0\), and the volume is \(45\pi\,\mathrm{cm^3}\).

Find the length \(h\) and the radius of the circular end at \(x=h\).
starters.hint: Keep the unknown upper limit while integrating the square of the radius. Apply the positive-length condition to the resulting quadratic roots.
starters.solution:
1. \[45\pi=\pi\int_0^h(4x+9)\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi(2h^2+9h).\]
  2. \[2h^2+9h-45=0\Longleftrightarrow(h-3)(2h+15)=0.\]
  3. \[h=3\quad\text{or}\quad h=-\frac{15}{2}.\]

  4. The physical length is positive, so \(h=3\,\mathrm{cm}\). The other algebraic root does not describe the stated solid.

  5. \[R(h)=\sqrt{4(3)+9}=\sqrt{21}\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

  6. Check the volume: \(\pi\bigl(2(3)^2+9(3)\bigr)=45\pi\,\mathrm{cm^3}\). The radius is real and positive throughout the selected interval.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the disk integral with an unknown upper limit.
  • 1 mark: integrate the squared radius correctly.
  • 1 mark: obtain and solve the volume equation.
  • 1 mark: select the positive physical length.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the end radius.
  • 1 mark: state the requested lengths with units and verify the physical interval.

revision.body:
Volume comes from the area of each perpendicular cross-section, not from the gap between graph heights.

Choose the axis and the cross-section

\[V_x=\pi\int_a^b(R^2-r^2)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]\[V_y=\pi\int_c^d(R^2-r^2)\,\mathrm{d}y.\]

About the \(x\)-axis, radii are vertical distances and limits are in \(x\). About the \(y\)-axis, use horizontal distances, boundaries in terms of \(y\) and limits in \(y\).

Square each radius before subtracting

For an axis-to-curve region, \(r=0\): the section is a disk. A hole gives a washer with \(0\le r\le R\).

\[A=\pi(R^2-r^2),\quad\text{not generally }\pi(R-r)^2.\]

Use distances, including below or left of an axis. Retain the actual inverse branch and the supplied region boundaries.

Split when the cross-section changes

A strip crossing the axis gives one disk, with radius equal to the greater endpoint distance. Do not add overlapping rotations of its two sides.

Split where a hole appears or disappears, the farther boundary changes, or a different curve supplies a boundary. Add volumes of separate slices only once.

Check a physical model

Choose interior capacity or material volume as requested. Solve the volume equation, retain all roots, then check positivity, domain and radius order. Substitute the accepted values back.

Use consistent lengths and cubic volume units; \(1000\,\mathrm{cm}^3=1\,\mathrm{L}\). Keep exact \(\pi\) where required. Singular or infinite boundaries need a convergence check for the volume integral.
revision.checks:
• Axis, slice direction and limits agree?
  • Radii measured from the axis, with the correct hole?
  • Squared radii subtracted and every slice counted once?
  • All roots, original domains and cubic units checked?

orig_integration_accumulation.description: Recover functions from higher derivatives, translate each condition into the right equation, and use signed rates to track changing amounts.

sections.title: Why do two integrations need two constants?
sections.label: Recovering from a second derivative
sections.intro: A second derivative tells you how the gradient changes. Integrating once recovers the first derivative with one arbitrary constant. Integrating again recovers the function and introduces another, independent constant.

blocks.html:
\[f^{\prime\prime}=g,\qquad f^{\prime}=G+C_1,\qquad f=H+C_1x+C_2,\]\[G^{\prime}=g,\qquad H^{\prime}=G.\]

The first constant becomes a linear term after the second integration. The new constant controls a vertical shift. Use separate names until the supplied conditions determine them.

1. Integrate \(f''(x)=2\) twice, keeping a new constant each time.\[f'(x)=2x+A,\qquad f(x)=x^2+Ax+B.\]
  2. The gradient condition \(f'(1)=1\) gives \(2+A=1\), so \(A=-1\).
  3. Use the point condition \(f(1)=4\) to obtain \(1-1+B=4\), so \(B=4\). Check by differentiating \(f(x)=x^2-x+4\).

For \(f^{\prime\prime}=2\), the family is \(f=x^2+Ax+B\). The gradient condition fixes \(A\); the point condition then fixes \(B\).

blocks.title: Keep a different constant at each integration
blocks.prompt: A function satisfies \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6\), \(f^{\prime}(0)=-2\) and \(f(0)=5\). Write \(f^{\prime}(x)=6x+A\) and \(f(x)=3x^2+Ax+B\). Find \(A\), \(B\) and \(f(2)\).
blocks.hint: The gradient condition belongs in \(f^{\prime}\); the height condition belongs in \(f\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(0)=A=-2,\qquad f(0)=B=5.\]
  2. \[f(x)=3x^2-2x+5,\qquad f(2)=12-4+5=13.\]

  3. Differentiating twice returns \(6\). The first constant became the linear term \(-2x\) in the function.

blocks.html:
Do not reuse one constant for both integrations or drop the first constant when integrating again:

\[\int C_1\,\mathrm{d}x=C_1x+C_2.\]

sections.title: Which expression should each condition go into?
sections.label: Heights, gradients and stationary points
sections.intro: Write each condition as an equation before substituting numbers. A height and a gradient at the same input are different pieces of information.

blocks.html:
• A point \((a,b)\) gives \(f(a)=b\).
  • A tangent gradient \(m\) at \(a\) gives \(f^{\prime}(a)=m\).
  • A stationary point \((a,b)\) gives both \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) and \(f(a)=b\).

A stationary point does not generally have zero second derivative. Use \(f^{\prime\prime}\) to classify it when that test is conclusive.

blocks.title: A stationary point gives a direction and a height
blocks.prompt: A curve has \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12x-2\) and a stationary point at \((1,1)\). After two integrations, write \(f(x)=2x^3-x^2+Ax+B\). Find \(A\) and \(B\), then classify the given stationary point.
blocks.hint: Use \(f^{\prime}(1)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\) as two separate equations.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=6x^2-2x+A,\qquad f^{\prime}(1)=4+A=0\Longrightarrow A=-4.\]
  2. \[f(1)=2-1-4+B=1\Longrightarrow B=4.\]
  3. \[f^{\prime\prime}(1)=10>0.\]

    The stationary point is a local minimum. Both its height and zero gradient hold in the recovered function.

blocks.html: Two independent conditions can determine the two constants after repeated integration. An extra unknown coefficient may need another independent condition. Repeating the same gradient information does not fix a missing height. Keep the original interval and any excluded inputs throughout.

Differentiate the recovered function twice and check every original condition separately. If the conditions leave a constant free or contradict one another, state that instead of forcing a unique curve.

sections.title: How do I use unknown coefficients and definite-integral conditions?
sections.label: Linked constants and integrals
sections.intro: A coefficient already present in the given derivative is different from a new integration constant. Hold all such parameters constant while integrating. Then use point, gradient or integral conditions to build simultaneous equations.

blocks.title: A point and an integral determine different unknowns
blocks.prompt: A function satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=2kx\), \(f(0)=2\) and \(\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=3\). Write \(f(x)=kx^2+C\). Find \(C\) and \(k\).
blocks.hint: The point fixes \(C\). That constant then contributes \(C\) times the interval width to the integral.
blocks.solution:
1. \[f(0)=C=2.\]
  2. \[\int_0^1(kx^2+2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[\frac{kx^3}{3}+2x\right]_0^1=\frac{k}{3}+2=3.\]
  3. \[k=3,\qquad f(x)=3x^2+2.\]

    Its derivative is \(6x\), and its integral on the given interval is \(1+2=3\).

blocks.html:
A constant inside the function being integrated does not vanish in a definite integral:

\[\int_a^b C\,\mathrm{d}x=C(b-a).\]

Only an added constant in the antiderivative cancels in the endpoint subtraction. Do not discard the unknown height term in \(f\).
Keep the same parameter values across all conditions on the stated interval. Solve the equations together, then substitute the results back into every original point or integral condition.

sections.title: How can a known derivative help me integrate?
sections.label: Recognising derivative multiples
sections.intro: If a question gives a function to differentiate and then asks for a related integral, compare the complete derivative with the integrand. They may differ by a constant factor. Include the inner derivative when making this comparison.

blocks.html:
If \(F^{\prime}(x)=g(x)\) and \(\lambda\) is constant, then

\[\int\lambda g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\lambda F(x)+C,\]\[\int_a^b\lambda g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\lambda\bigl(F(b)-F(a)\bigr).\]

Check the proposed result by differentiation on the original domain.

blocks.title: Recognise a constant multiple of a known derivative
blocks.prompt: Let \(F(x)=(x^3+1)^2\). Write \(3x^2(x^3+1)=\lambda F^{\prime}(x)\), then use this to evaluate \(\int_0^1 3x^2(x^3+1)\,\mathrm{d}x\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the proposed function first. The inner derivative is \(3x^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[F^{\prime}(x)=2(x^3+1)(3x^2)=6x^2(x^3+1),\qquad\lambda=\frac{1}{2}.\]
  2. \[\int_0^1 3x^2(x^3+1)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{2}[F(1)-F(0)]=\frac{1}{2}(4-1)=\frac{3}{2}.\]

  3. The factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) multiplies the whole endpoint difference.

blocks.html: The matching factor must be constant. If a factor involving \(x\) is missing, you cannot repair the integral by multiplying by a numerical constant. Expand a polynomial where practical, or use a derivative actually established by the question.

sections.title: How does a changing rate determine the amount present?
sections.label: Net accumulation and extrema
sections.intro: Integrating a net rate gives a change, not automatically the final amount. For a tank, use inflow minus outflow. A negative net rate means the amount is falling, even if the amount itself is still positive.

blocks.html:
\[Q^{\prime}(t)=q(t),\qquad Q(t)=Q(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.\]

The letter \(s\) is the variable inside the integral; \(t\) is the requested finishing time. Rate multiplied by time has the unit of the accumulated amount.

For \(Q'(t)=6-2t\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}\) and \(Q(0)=5\,\mathrm{L}\), add the signed change to the initial amount.

\[Q(t)=5+\int_0^t(6-2u)\,\mathrm{d}u=5+6t-t^2.\]

At \(t=5\) the amount is \(5+9-4=10\,\mathrm{L}\). The maximum occurs at \(t=3\) because the rate changes from positive to negative there.

The net rate \(6-2t\) becomes zero at \(t=3\). The amount \(5+6t-t^2\) is then greatest, at \(14\,\mathrm{L}\), and later decreases to \(10\,\mathrm{L}\).

blocks.title: Find the amount, not only its net change
blocks.prompt: A tank initially contains \(3\,\mathrm{L}\). Its net rate of change is \(q(t)=(4-t)\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}\) for \(0\le t\le6\), where \(t\) is measured in minutes. Find the amount after six minutes and the greatest amount on this interval, together with the time when it occurs.
blocks.hint: Add the integrated net rate to the initial amount. The amount can have an interior maximum where the net rate changes from positive to negative.
blocks.solution:
1. \[V(t)=3+\int_0^t(4-s)\,\mathrm{d}s=3+4t-\frac{t^2}{2}.\]
  2. \[V(6)=3+24-18=9\,\mathrm{L}.\]
  3. \[q(t)=0\Longrightarrow t=4.\]

    The rate is positive before this time and negative after it.

  4. \[V(0)=3,\qquad V(4)=11,\qquad V(6)=9.\]

    The greatest amount is \(11\,\mathrm{L}\), at \(4\,\mathrm{min}\). These amounts remain physically nonnegative throughout the stated interval.

blocks.html: To find a global maximum or minimum on a closed time interval, compare the amount at both endpoints and at every allowed stationary time where \(q(t)=0\). Include any other points where the model changes or the derivative is undefined. Keep every time that attains the same extreme value.
The greatest rate and the greatest amount need not occur together. Do not replace the signed net-rate integral by an integral of \(|q|\): that adds gains and losses instead of giving the net change.

Use the stated time interval and consistent units. A physical amount must respect the model’s restrictions, such as nonnegative contents and any capacity limit. Do not extend the formula beyond those restrictions without a new model.

glossary.definition: Integrating more than once to recover lower derivatives and then the original function.
Separate arbitrary values introduced by separate integrations.
Given information about a function, derivative or integral that supplies an equation for unknowns.
A fixed but possibly unknown coefficient that is held constant while integrating.
The amount already present at the starting time.
The signed rate of increase after subtracting decreases, such as inflow minus outflow.
The change obtained by integrating a rate over time.
The temporary variable inside a definite integral; its name does not change the value.

examples.title: Recover both the gradient and the function
examples.question: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=2\), \(f^{\prime}(1)=1\) and \(f(1)=4\). Find its equation.
solution:
Integrate once and introduce the first constant:

\[f^{\prime}(x)=2x+A.\]
\[f^{\prime}(1)=2+A=1\Longrightarrow A=-1.\]

Integrate the complete first derivative and introduce a new constant:

\[f(x)=x^2-x+B.\]
\[f(1)=1-1+B=4\Longrightarrow B=4.\]

\[f(x)=x^2-x+4.\]

Its second derivative is \(2\), its gradient at \(1\) is \(1\), and its height there is \(4\).

examples.title: Translate a stationary point into two equations
examples.question: A curve has \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12x\) and a stationary point at \((1,3)\). Find the curve and classify that point.
solution: \[f^{\prime}(x)=6x^2+A,\qquad f(x)=2x^3+Ax+B.\]

A stationary point has zero first derivative:

\[f^{\prime}(1)=6+A=0\Longrightarrow A=-6.\]

Its stated height belongs in the function:

\[f(1)=2-6+B=3\Longrightarrow B=7.\]
\[f(x)=2x^3-6x+7,\qquad f^{\prime\prime}(1)=12>0.\]
The given point is a local minimum. Differentiating twice and checking \(f^{\prime}(1)=0\), \(f(1)=3\) verifies every original condition.

examples.title: Keep an unknown coefficient while recovering a curve
examples.question: A function satisfies \(f^{\prime}(x)=2kx+3\), \(f(0)=1\) and \(\int_0^2f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{40}{3}\). Find \(k\) and the function.
solution:
Treat \(k\) as constant when integrating:

\[f(x)=kx^2+3x+C.\]
\[f(0)=1\Longrightarrow C=1.\]
\[\frac{8k}{3}+8=\frac{40}{3}\Longrightarrow k=2.\]

\[f(x)=2x^2+3x+1.\]

The derivative is \(4x+3\), the initial height is \(1\), and the required integral is \(\frac{16}{3}+8=\frac{40}{3}\).

examples.title: Two definite integrals can determine a whole linear function
examples.question: A function has constant derivative \(f^{\prime}(x)=a\). Given \(\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=4\) and \(\int_1^2f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=7\), find \(f(x)\).
solution:
The first integral gives

\[\left[\frac{ax^2}{2}+Cx\right]_0^1=\frac{a}{2}+C=4.\]

The second integral gives a different equation:

\[\left[\frac{ax^2}{2}+Cx\right]_1^2=\frac{3a}{2}+C=7.\]

Subtract the equations to obtain \(a=3\). Then

\[C=4-\frac{3}{2}=\frac{5}{2}.\]

\[f(x)=3x+\frac{5}{2}.\]

Its two integrals are \(\frac{3}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=4\) and \(\frac{9}{2}+\frac{5}{2}=7\), as required.

examples.title: Use a derivative that has already been identified
examples.question: Let \(F(x)=(x^2+2)^3\). Differentiate \(F\), then find \(\int2x(x^2+2)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\int_0^1 2x(x^2+2)^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
solution:
The chain rule gives

\[F^{\prime}(x)=3(x^2+2)^2(2x)=6x(x^2+2)^2.\]

The required integrand is one third of this derivative:

\[2x(x^2+2)^2=\frac{1}{3}F^{\prime}(x).\]
Differentiating the proposed antiderivative confirms the factor. Expanding the integrand and integrating its powers would give the same definite value.

examples.title: Combine an initial amount with a changing net rate
examples.question: A tank starts with \(5\,\mathrm{L}\). Water enters at \(6\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}\) and leaves at \(2t\,\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}\), for \(0\le t\le5\). Find the amount after five minutes and the maximum amount during this interval.
solution:
The net rate is inflow minus outflow:

\[Q^{\prime}(t)=6-2t.\]

Add the accumulated change to the initial amount:

\[Q(t)=5+\int_0^t(6-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s=5+6t-t^2.\]

\[Q(5)=5+30-25=10\,\mathrm{L}.\]

The net change is \(5\,\mathrm{L}\); the final amount includes the \(5\,\mathrm{L}\) present initially.

The amount increases while the net rate is positive and decreases while it is negative:

\[6-2t=0\Longrightarrow t=3.\]
The maximum is \(14\,\mathrm{L}\) at \(t=3\,\mathrm{min}\). The model stays nonnegative on the stated interval. At the maximum amount, inflow and outflow are equal; the amount itself is not zero.

extraPractice.title: Two integrations need two separate constants
extraPractice.prompt: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=12x-6\), \(f^{\prime}(1)=5\) and \(f(1)=2\). Recover it in the form \(f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+d\), finding all four coefficients.
extraPractice.hint: The gradient condition fixes the first integration constant. Its contribution becomes a linear term in the recovered function.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=6x^2-6x+A,\qquad f^{\prime}(1)=A=5.\]
  2. \[f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+5x+B.\]
  3. \[2=f(1)=2-3+5+B\Longrightarrow B=-2.\]
  4. \[f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+5x-2.\]

  5. Differentiating twice gives the supplied second derivative. Substitution also verifies both original conditions.

extraPractice.title: Two height conditions can determine the two constants
extraPractice.prompt: A curve satisfies \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x\), \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(2)=5\). Write it as \(f(x)=x^3+Ax+B\). Find \(A,B\) and the gradient at \(x=2\).
extraPractice.hint: Integrate twice before using the two height conditions. A condition on the function does not belong in its derivative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+A,\qquad f(x)=x^3+Ax+B.\]
  2. \[f(0)=1\Longrightarrow B=1,\qquad5=8+2A+1\Longrightarrow A=-2.\]
  3. \[f(x)=x^3-2x+1,\qquad f^{\prime}(2)=3(2)^2-2=10.\]

extraPractice.title: Determine a coefficient before classifying the recovered curve
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has constant second derivative \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)=k\), with \(f^{\prime}(0)=-3\), \(f(1)=2\) and \(f(3)=6\). Write it as \(f(x)=\frac{k}{2}x^2-3x+B\). Find \(k,B\) and the minimum point.
extraPractice.hint: The initial gradient fixes the linear coefficient. Subtract the two point equations to find \(k\), then recover \(B\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=kx-3,\qquad f(x)=\frac{k}{2}x^2-3x+B.\]
  2. \[2=\frac{k}{2}-3+B,\qquad6=\frac{9k}{2}-9+B.\]
  3. \[4=4k-6\Longrightarrow k=\frac{5}{2},\qquad B=\frac{15}{4}.\]
  4. \[f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{5}{2}x-3=0\Longrightarrow x=\frac{6}{5}.\]
  5. \[f\left(\frac{6}{5}\right)=\frac{39}{20}.\]

  6. The second derivative is the positive constant \(\frac{5}{2}\), so this stationary point is a minimum of the upward-opening quadratic.

extraPractice.title: Recognise a verified derivative and restore its multiplier
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(F(x)=(x^2+1)^4\). Differentiate it, then use that result to find \(K\) in

\[\int3x(x^2+1)^3\,\mathrm{d}x=KF(x)+C.\]

Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 3x(x^2+1)^3\,\mathrm{d}x\) exactly.

retry.feedback: The outer derivative supplies \(4\), but the inner derivative supplies another factor \(2x\). Compare with the full derivative \(8x(x^2+1)^3\).

extraPractice.hint: The chain rule supplies the inner derivative \(2x\). Compare the whole derivative with the required integrand.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[F^{\prime}(x)=4(x^2+1)^3(2x)=8x(x^2+1)^3.\]
  2. \[3x(x^2+1)^3=\frac{3}{8}F^{\prime}(x)\Longrightarrow K=\frac{3}{8}.\]
  3. \[\int_0^1 3x(x^2+1)^3\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{3}{8}\bigl(F(1)-F(0)\bigr)=\frac{3}{8}(16-1)=\frac{45}{8}.\]

  4. The method reverses an explicitly checked derivative relation. No change of integration variable is needed.

extraPractice.title: Separate net change, final amount and greatest amount
extraPractice.prompt:
A tank contains \(10\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) at \(t=0\). Its net rate of volume change is \(q(t)=8-2t\), measured in \(\mathrm{cm^3\,min^{-1}}\), for \(0\le t\le6\), with \(t\) in minutes.

Find the net change over this interval, the final volume, and the greatest volume with the time at which it occurs.

retry.feedback: This is the net change. Add the initial \(10\,\mathrm{cm^3}\) to obtain the final amount.

extraPractice.hint: Add the integral of the rate to the initial amount. Use the sign of the rate and the interval endpoints to find the greatest amount.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V(t)=10+\int_0^t(8-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s=10+8t-t^2.\]
  2. \[\Delta V=\int_0^6(8-2t)\,\mathrm{d}t=12\,\mathrm{cm^3},\qquad V(6)=22\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]
  3. \[q(t)=0\Longrightarrow t=4,\qquad V(4)=26\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  4. The rate is positive before \(4\) and negative after it, so the volume increases then decreases. The endpoint volumes are \(V(0)=10\) and \(V(6)=22\), both below \(26\). The stated model remains nonnegative throughout its interval.

starters.title: A definite-integral condition fixes an unknown curve parameter
starters.question:
A curve satisfies

\[f^{\prime\prime}(x)=6x+a,\qquad f^{\prime}(0)=-1,\qquad f(1)=2,\qquad\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1.\]

Let \(b=f(0)\). Find \(a,b\), state the complete equation of the curve and find \(f^{\prime}(1)\).
starters.hint: After two integrations, the point condition and integral condition give two equations in \(a,b\). The parameter already present in the integrand does not disappear when the new antiderivative constant cancels.
starters.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=3x^2+ax-1,\qquad f(x)=x^3+\frac{a}{2}x^2-x+b.\]
  2. \[f(1)=2\Longrightarrow\frac{a}{2}+b=2.\]
  3. \[\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{a}{6}-\frac{1}{2}+b=1\Longrightarrow\frac{a}{6}+b=\frac{5}{4}.\]
  4. \[\frac{a}{3}=\frac{3}{4}\Longrightarrow a=\frac{9}{4},\qquad b=2-\frac{9}{8}=\frac{7}{8}.\]
  5. \[f(x)=x^3+\frac{9}{8}x^2-x+\frac{7}{8},\qquad f^{\prime}(1)=3+\frac{9}{4}-1=\frac{17}{4}.\]

  6. Differentiating twice returns \(6x+\frac{9}{4}\). Direct substitution verifies the initial gradient, the point at \(x=1\) and the signed integral condition.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: recover the first derivative and use its initial condition.
  • 1 mark: recover the function with a second constant.
  • 1 mark: form the point equation.
  • 1 mark: form the definite-integral equation without losing the parameter in the integrand.
  • 1 mark: solve the simultaneous equations for both unknowns.
  • 1 mark: state the full recovered curve.
  • 1 mark: obtain the requested gradient and check the original conditions.

starters.title: An endpoint can tie with an interior maximum
starters.question:
An accumulated amount \(A(t)\), measured in cubic centimetres, is modelled for \(0\le t\le4\), with time in minutes. It satisfies

\[A^{\prime\prime}(t)=6t-12,\qquad A^{\prime}(0)=9,\qquad A(0)=5.\]

Here derivatives use minutes as the time unit. Recover \(A(t)\). Find its greatest and least values on the whole interval, every time when each is attained, and its net change from \(0\) to \(4\).
starters.hint: Use a fresh constant at each integration. Find stationary times from the rate, then compare all allowed stationary values and both endpoints. Keep ties.
starters.solution:
1. \[A^{\prime}(t)=3t^2-12t+C_1,\qquad C_1=9.\]
  2. \[A(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t+C_2,\qquad C_2=5.\]
  3. \[A^{\prime}(t)=3(t-1)(t-3)=0\Longrightarrow t=1,3.\]

  4. The rate is positive on \((0,1)\), negative on \((1,3)\) and positive on \((3,4)\). Compare the stationary times with both included endpoints.

  5. \[A(0)=5,\quad A(1)=9,\quad A(3)=5,\quad A(4)=9.\]

  6. The greatest amount is \(9\,\mathrm{cm^3}\), attained at both \(1\) and \(4\) minutes. The least is \(5\,\mathrm{cm^3}\), attained at both \(0\) and \(3\) minutes. These bounds also show the quantity stays nonnegative throughout the model interval.

  7. \[\Delta A=A(4)-A(0)=9-5=4\,\mathrm{cm^3}.\]

  8. The two integration constants represent different missing conditions. Net change is a difference of amounts; it is not the greatest amount reached during the interval.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: integrate the second derivative and determine the first constant.
  • 1 mark: integrate again and determine the second constant.
  • 1 mark: obtain every allowed stationary time.
  • 1 mark: establish the rate sign pattern.
  • 1 mark: compare both stationary values and both endpoint values.
  • 1 mark: state the greatest amount with all its attaining times.
  • 1 mark: state the least amount with all its attaining times.
  • 1 mark: obtain the net change.
  • 1 mark: retain the whole stated interval, correct units and a physically nonnegative amount.

revision.body:
Each integration introduces a new constant; each condition must be applied to the correct quantity.

Integrate twice and retain both constants

\[f^{\prime}=G+C_1,\qquad f=H+C_1x+C_2,\]\[G^{\prime}=f^{\prime\prime},\qquad H^{\prime}=G.\]

The first constant becomes a linear term. Use independent names and preserve the original domain. Differentiate twice to check the result.

Translate and link the conditions

Height: \(f(a)=b\). Gradient: \(f^{\prime}(a)=m\). Stationary point: both \(f^{\prime}(a)=0\) and the given height.

Hold unknown coefficients constant while integrating. Point and definite-integral conditions can form simultaneous equations. A constant inside \(f\) contributes \(C(b-a)\) to its integral; it does not cancel like an added antiderivative constant.

Recognise a derivative multiple

\[F^{\prime}=g\Longrightarrow\int\lambda g\,\mathrm{d}x=\lambda F+C.\]

The factor \(\lambda\) must be constant. For definite limits, use \(\lambda(F(b)-F(a))\). Keep the complete inner-derivative factor and verify by differentiation.

Accumulate the net change

\[Q(t)=Q(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s.\]

Use the signed net rate and include the initial amount. Positive rate increases the amount; negative rate decreases it.

Compare endpoint amounts and all allowed stationary times, plus any model-change points. Retain ties for global extremes. Check the stated time interval, physical restrictions and matching units.
revision.checks:
• New independent constant for each integration?
  • Each height, gradient and integral condition used correctly?
  • Complete derivative match and all original equations checked?
  • Initial amount, signed change, endpoint comparisons and units included?
